text:
Erika Acosta wonders anxiously how her 67-year-old mother-in-law Linda will treat her diabetes and other health issues in the rural El Salvador village she left decades ago but is being forced to move back to next week.

The temporary immigration status that allowed certain Salvadoran immigrants like Linda, who is using a pseudonym to protect her identity, to live in the U.S. expires on September 9.

“I’m stressed out,” Acosta, a property manager who lives in Glendale, told LA Public Press. “She takes 12 medications per month. I don’t want to send her back.”

For 26 years, Linda has had authorization to live and work in the country under a federal program called Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, Acosta said.

Historically, the TPS program has allowed people from certain countries to work in the U.S. if the government deemed those places unsafe for return due to ongoing armed conflicts, environmental disasters, or “extraordinary and temporary conditions.”

The Trump administration said in an Aug. 12 notice that it’s ending TPS for Salvadorans. The decision will impact about 170,000 people across the country.

The administration has already ended the program for a dozen countries including Haiti, Nepal, and Honduras. The terminations affected more than 1 million people, including 600,000 from Venezuela.

The Department of Homeland Security could issue a decision to extend Salvadoran TPS, but if a decision is not made by Sept. 9, TPS for Salvadorans should automatically extend for six months, according to federal law.

LA County is home to more than 452,000 Salvadorans, according to the 2020 Census. It’s unclear how many Salvadoran TPS holders live in LA County.

Acosta said she and her husband haven’t been able to obtain permanent legal status for Linda, despite spending years and thousands of dollars to do so. She’s concerned Linda won’t be able to get proper medical care in El Salvador or navigate a country she hasn’t lived in for 33 years.

“She’ll die,” Acosta said. “What can we do? We’ve tried to do everything.”

Individuals who lose TPS protection have details about their location and immigration status filed with the U.S. government and might be at risk of arrest by federal immigration agents, according to the nonprofit legal aid organization Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project. The organization states on their website that the risk of arrest is heightened if people don’t have some other legal immigration status.

The Department of Homeland Security didn’t respond to an LA Public Press email asking whether the federal agency plans to target Salvadorans losing TPS for arrest or whether it plans to extend TPS protections.

TPS shielded immigrants from deportation and allowed them to work legally

Congress created TPS in 1990 to protect certain vetted immigrants from deportation and provide them work permits if their home countries were unsafe.

TPS, which can be granted for up to 18 months, also allows people to apply for permission to travel outside the U.S. with the ability to return. Because the federal government has designated TPS for El Salvador since 2001, some Salvadorans like Linda built a life in the U.S for decades, albeit tenuously, by continuously reapplying for TPS.

Acosta said Linda typically paid about $500 every 18 months to renew TPS.

In June, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority ruled 6 to 3 that the Trump administration has broad authority to eliminate TPS.

Guillermo Torres, an organizer at the nonprofit interfaith organization Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice, or CLUE, told LA Public Press he worries about people being forced to return to countries with ongoing political instability or violence.

“Ever since this administration came back, we’ve seen horrific cruelty and evil and heartless policies,” said Torres, who is CLUE’s director of programs for immigration justice. “Are we going to let this administration deport all these community members possibly back to their deaths, possibly back to violence?”

El Salvador’s populist president Nayib Bukele has said his country is safer after he instituted a controversial and widespread security crackdown that imprisoned more than 90,000 people. Human Rights Watch said in a 2022 report that Bukele’s security plan resulted in human rights violations against his country’s people, including arbitrary arrests, disappearances, and torture.

Bukele has been accused by human rights advocates of illegally removing the county’s high court judges and seeking a third consecutive term, a move some have called unconstitutional.

Asked what faith leaders can do to protect Salvadorans who are forced to return to El Salvador, Torres said CLUE is asking its network to offer sanctuary inside houses of worship to individuals losing TPS.

“There has to be more action, more protection, including taking immigrants into safe spaces inside the churches to shelter them and to push back on this administration,” Torres said. “Hopefully this administration isn’t going to violate the house of god.”

Margaret Cargioli, advocacy and external relations director at Immigrant Defenders Law Center, told LA Public Press the Trump administration is advancing its campaign of mass deportations by ending TPS, but it’s tearing communities apart by doing so.

“People with [TPS] have been part of the fabric of the U.S.,” Cargioli said. “There are hundreds of thousands of workers with TPS that contribute to our economy and participate in our communities. This will uproot families and impact the employment sector.”

What you should do if your TPS is ending, and how to support TPS holders

Individuals who are losing TPS may consider applying for asylum. If asylum isn’t an option for former TPS holders, they can work with an attorney to determine their eligibility for a different immigration status, according to the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project.

Cargioli said immigrants losing TPS or who don’t have another immigration status should create an emergency plan in case a family member is deported or detained.

The emergency plan should include methods for creating copies of important documents, storing copies of vital documents with trusted individuals, preparing financial accounts in case families need to pay an immigration bond, and planning for the care of children if families are separated.

“These immigration tactics are not only harming immigrants, they’re harming U.S. citizen children of immigrants that are being impacted by these harsh and fruitless immigration tactics,” Cargioli said.

She said advocates for immigrants can also donate to bond funds and legal aid organizations and demand that Congress take action to protect people with TPS.

“Congress can act and legislate to help people, who have been here in the United States for almost their entire lives, to remain here lawfully, and stop allowing these egregious actions that tear families apart,” Cargioli said.

title: Transnational repression: a world without refuge - CIVICUS LENS
description:
The law is the latest expression of transnational repression, a practice where China is the global leader.
A growing practice Transnational repression is what happens when a government reaches beyond its borders to intimidate, punish and silence its citizens living elsewhere.
Transnational violence The most extreme expression of transnational repression is the murder of exiles.
These moves offered a welcome break from the tendency of global north democracies to condemn transnational repression without penalising perpetrators.
According to the International Partnership for Human Rights, the European Union’s Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime is poorly suited to tackling transnational repression, as it only applies to serious violations such as killing and torture, while most transnational repression works through subtler means.
text:
As authoritarianism expands, more activists are being forced into exile, but repression is following them. Repressive states are reaching across borders to silence critics who’ve fled. Tactics continue to evolve, with recent instances of states outsourcing killings to criminal networks, cooperating to hunt down dissidents and weaponising international agreements on crime and deportation. While China continues to lead the way, more states than ever are practising transnational repression, and democratic host states are increasingly enabling it through their asylum and immigration systems. Those forced to seek safety abroad urgently need more support.

In July, China’s ‘Ethnic Unity Law’ came into effect, giving the authorities new powers to suppress dissent it deems a threat to national unity. Crucially, the law makes clear that China will target dissidents abroad, stating that individuals and groups outside the country may be held liable if they ‘undermine ethnic unity’ or ‘create ethnic division’. The law is the latest expression of transnational repression, a practice where China is the global leader.

A growing practice

Transnational repression is what happens when a government reaches beyond its borders to intimidate, punish and silence its citizens living elsewhere. Those targeted – civil society activists, dissidents, human rights defenders, journalists and members of the political opposition – have often gone into exile to continue work they can no longer do due to civic space restrictions at home. But repression follows them, aimed at stopping them speaking out, raising awareness of human rights violations and supporting those who remain in their home country.

And it’s on the rise. As civic space is increasingly restricted and more states slide towards authoritarianism, more people are forced into exile, and governments seek to silence them. Freedom House, which has recorded physical incidents of transnational repression since 2014, documented 126 new cases in 2025, bringing its running total to 1,375. At least 54 states have engaged in transnational repression, with six — Afghanistan, Benin, Georgia, Kenya, Tanzania and Zimbabwe — identified as using these tactics for the first time in 2025.

Ten states account for over 70 per cent of all incidents, with China, Vietnam and Russia the three worst offenders. China is responsible for 319 recorded instances of physical transnational repression. It pursues Hong Kong democracy activists and Tibetans, Uyghurs and other minorities it regards as enemies of the state. Its campaign extends to Taiwanese civil society activists and elected officials, treated as Chinese nationals under its ‘One China’ principle, which views Taiwan not as an independent country but as a rebellious Chinese province.

China’s reach is wide. A university student was reportedly jailed for six years after returning home from Australia, where he took part in a protest. A dissident disappeared in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE), likely kidnapped and returned to China.

China also uses its economic power to silence dissent far from home. In April, Zambia – a country that owes China billions of dollars – abruptly called off RightsCon, a global digital rights conference, evidently yielding to Chinese pressure over the participation of Taiwanese activists. In August, Chinese diplomatic pressure tried to force the cancellation of a human rights conference in Buenos Aires, Argentina, when the Chinese Ambassador directly contacted the Argentine government over the scheduled participation of prominent exiled Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa. The city government cancelled the meeting venue, forcing it to take place at a different location.

Transnational violence

The most extreme expression of transnational repression is the murder of exiles. In June 2025, former Nicaraguan army major Roberto Samcam was shot dead at his home near San José, Costa Rica. Samcam was an outspoken critic of Nicaraguan dictator Daniel Ortega and had lived in exile since fleeing repression in 2018. His killing was at least the third of a Nicaraguan exile in Costa Rica in recent years. Other Nicaraguan exiles living in the country have been shot at and beaten, and intelligence services have warned journalists that their lives are in danger. The message for the hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguans in Costa Rica is clear: there’s no safety in exile, because the government they’ve fled can still reach them.

Under former President Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela pursued its opponents abroad with similar determination. In October 2025, gunmen in Bogotá, Colombia’s capital, opened fire on two exiled Venezuelan activists, Luis Peche and Yendri Velásquez. Velásquez was hit eight times and Peche six, but both somehow survived.

Repressive states are increasingly contracting out transnational violence, hiring organised crime syndicates to conduct assassinations abroad, a method that provides plausible deniability. In February 2024, men in fake police uniforms abducted exiled Venezuelan ex-army lieutenant Ronald Ojeda from his apartment in Santiago de Chile. His dismembered body was found in a suitcase buried under concrete nine days later. Chilean prosecutors concluded that the killing was politically motivated, ordered by the Venezuelan government and carried out by a Venezuelan gang. Chile has briefed the International Criminal Court on the case as part of its investigation into the Maduro government.

Iran has repeatedly used similar methods. In March 2025, a New York jury convicted two members of an Eastern European crime ring hired by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard for a 2022 plot to kill exiled journalist Masih Alinejad at her Brooklyn home. Another plot to kill her during a speaking engagement at Fairfield University in Connecticut was run by an Iranian operative who recruited two US men to carry out the assassination through criminal contacts. In the UK, two Romanian nationals were convicted of a knife attack on exiled Iranian television presenter Pouria Zeraati. Prosecutors established that they were hired criminal proxies for the Iranian regime.

India has faced similar accusations. US prosecutors indicted an Indian national who worked with a former Indian intelligence officer to hire an assassin to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a Sikh separatist leader in New York. The plot was foiled when the hitman turned out to be an undercover agent. The indictment tied the plot to the June 2023 killing of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar, shot dead outside a temple in British Columbia, Canada.

Nicaraguan lawyer Marlon Medina shows a photograph of the vehicle in which opposition figure Joao Maldonado survived an assassination attempt during an interview in San José, Costa Rica, on 9 May 2026. Photo by Martin Bernetti/AFP.

Surveillance and intimidation

Before repression turns physical, states watch, intimidate and threaten exiles, including through their families at home. An International Consortium of Investigative Journalists investigation based on interviews with 105 Chinese exiles targeted for transnational repression across 23 countries found that half had seen relatives in China interrogated or intimidated by the authorities, often within hours of taking part in a protest abroad. In February, the father of exiled Hong Kong activist Anna Kwok received an eight-month sentence for violating national security laws after trying to cash in his daughter’s education savings insurance policy.

have carried out mass raids, asset seizures and forced televised confessions targeting the families of exiled opposition figures. Egyptian authorities have long raided homes and arbitrarily detained family members of campaigners based abroad, such as US-based activist Mohamed Soltan. In 2017, Bahrain imprisoned several close relatives of London-based human rights activist Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei in direct retaliation for his protests against the Bahraini king’s visit to the UK. Tajikistan and Uzbekistan routinely freeze bank accounts of exiled dissidents, conduct aggressive interrogations of their relatives and target their children and grandchildren by expelling them from universities, subjecting them to classroom harassment and blocking them from travelling abroad to attend school.

Targeting of families is often combined with other tactics. Saudi Arabia imprisons family members, imposes indefinite travel bans and deploys military-grade spyware against overseas critics. The Chinese government uses financial pressure, from freezing pensions to blocking bank accounts at home, to coerce those who flee, and has begun issuing exiled Hong Kong activists with spurious tax demands. Financial coercion is combined with surveillance and threats against exiled activists. When China’s President Xi Jinping visited France in May 2024, Uyghur activists who held a protest reported being attacked, threatened and placed under surveillance, and accused the Chinese embassy of orchestrating the repression.

Iran’s theocratic regime uses a similar set of tactics, pursuing exiles by confiscating their assets and threatening their relatives at home. Staff at BBC Persian in the UK have reported that family members in Iran have been detained to punish them. The trend has intensified during the country’s war with Israel and the USA.

The experience of exiled Iranians in the UK, once a relatively safe haven for political dissidents, is part of a broader pattern. Alongside China and Iran, states including Bahrain, Egypt, Eritrea, Pakistan, Russia and Rwanda have repeatedly deployed coercive tactics on British soil. These include direct physical assaults, spyware, predatory lawfare and the detention and intimidation of relatives back home.

Bounties, Red Notices and cancelled passports

Authoritarian states routinely turn international administrative and legal machinery against exiled critics. In 2023, Hong Kong police placed bounties of around US$130,000 on eight exiled pro-democracy figures, including former student leader Nathan Law, with Hong Kong’s leader John Lee vowing they’d be pursued for life. Authorities added six more names to the bounty list in December 2024 and 19 more in July 2025.

Autocracies systematically exploit Interpol’s global alert system to target dissidents. There are dozens of documented instances of states weaponising Red Notices – global alerts that request but don’t mandate arrests – against political opponents. Aysoltan Niyazova, a Turkmen activist and member of the Russian feminist punk band Pussy Riot, was subject to Red Notices for 24 years and repeatedly detained as a result before Interpol finally intervened to remove her from the list in February. In March 2025, Sudan’s Red Notice against Yassir Arman, a prominent political opposition figure, led to him being stopped at Nairobi airport in Kenya until authorities recognised the political nature of the alert and let him go.

The government of El Salvador has issued Red Notices against human rights lawyers living in exile in Spain, though condemnation from United Nations (UN) human rights experts forced Interpol to withdraw the alerts. Systems to prevent abuse remain weak. Despite Interpol’s announcement of improved vetting protocols following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, around 90 per cent of notices submitted by Russia over the following two years received initial approval.

Beyond policing alerts, authoritarian regimes increasingly use bureaucratic disenfranchisement and denationalisation to punish exiles. In 2024, Hong Kong authorities invoked national security powers to cancel the passports of exiled activists, including people based in Australia, Canada, the UK and the USA. Iran has also revoked the citizenship of exiles. Egypt weaponises consular bureaucracy, denying passport renewals and withholding birth certificates to leave exiles functionally stateless. In 2023, Nicaragua enacted constitutional and legal changes that allowed it to formally strip over 300 journalists, political opponents and expelled political prisoners of their citizenship. Alongside the loss of nationality, the government ordered the immediate confiscation of all local assets and properties of those targeted.

Cross-border collaboration

Authoritarian states are increasingly collaborating to capture and return exiles to countries where they’re certain to face detention and violence. Forced returns violate the principle of non-refoulement, which forbids sending people to countries where they risk persecution or torture, under the Refugee Convention and the Convention Against Torture.

Collaboration is clear in Southeast Asia, with Thailand a major hub. In 2025, Thai authorities deported 40 Uyghur men to China, where they face severe persecution, after holding them in immigration detention for over a decade. Thailand also forcibly returned Vietnamese human rights activist Y Quynh Bdap to face terrorism charges despite his official status as a refugee recognised by the UN, and it routinely detains Chinese dissidents and forces Cambodian opposition figures back across the border.

Repressive African regimes are increasingly collaborating to silence dissent, often trading favours with neighbouring states and exploiting weak asylum protections. In 2026, Tanzania’s President Samia Suluhu Hassan called for closer cooperation with Kenya to curb cross-border activism she portrayed as disruptive.

Kenya has become a hotspot. In 2024, Kenyan officials helped Ugandan agents abduct Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye in Nairobi, forcing him back to face trial in a military court. Athorbey Al-Gaddhaffy-Dit, a whistleblower with dual Kenyan and South Sudanese citizenship, was abducted in Kenya in June. In January 2025, Tanzanian security forces abducted exiled activist Maria Sarungi Tsehai in Nairobi, assaulted her and tried to unlock her phone. Months later, Tanzanian officers detained and tortured Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan lawyer Agather Atuhaire after they arrived in Tanzania to observe an opposition leader’s trial. Kenya has also expelled foreign rights workers, including Ugandan legal adviser Martin Mavenjina, over their advocacy.

In May 2025, Tanzanian authorities arrested and deported Abdousalam Ibrahim Mpingou, an activist from Comoros living in Tanzania, over his social media posts critical of the Comoros government. In West Africa, agents from Benin kidnapped digital activist Steve Amoussou from exile in Togo, while authorities in Côte d’Ivoire arrested journalist Comlan Hugues Sossoukpè and sent him back to Benin despite his refugee status.

Middle Eastern and North African states increasingly use bilateral and multilateral security channels to repress exiled dissidents. In December 2024, Lebanese authorities arrested Egyptian-Turkish poet and dissident Abdulrahman Yusuf al-Qaradawi as he returned from Syria in response to a provisional arrest request from Egypt. While he was in custody, the UAE filed an extradition request through the Arab Interior Ministers Council, citing a social media post in which al-Qaradawi criticised Emirati authorities and celebrated the fall of Syria’s Assad regime. Despite a pending appeal before Lebanon’s top administrative court, the Lebanese government extradited him to the UAE in January 2025, even though he isn’t an Emirati citizen and wasn’t on Emirati soil when the alleged offence occurred. UAE authorities have since held him largely incommunicado.

Following a similar pattern, Emirati dissident Jasem Al-Shamsi was arrested in Syria in November 2025 and transferred to an undisclosed location shortly after the UAE placed him on a domestic terrorism list and sentenced him in absentia. He remains forcibly disappeared.

In May, Saudi Arabia arrested Kuwaiti opposition figure Waleed Al-Tabtabaie and handed him back to Kuwait, where he’d been convicted in absentia over criticism of the country’s rulers. That same month, authorities in Oman detained Egyptian dissident Mariam Abdelbasette at a hospital, days after she gave birth, on the basis of what her lawyers say was a fabricated Interpol Red Notice. She and her baby were released following an international outcry, but her husband, Ahmed Mousa, had already been forcibly deported to Egypt and imprisoned. The Gulf Centre for Human Rights has documented over 20 such cases linked to seven states — Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE — between 2022 and 2026.

Turkey has ignored domestic judicial injunctions and deported Russian anti-war activists to Russia and Turkmen dissident bloggers to Turkmenistan. Kazakhstan continues to arrest and extradite activists to Uzbekistan.

Belarus and Russia, meanwhile, appear to be moving against each other’s targets. In August 2025, Belarusian dissident Anatol Kotau, wanted in Russia, disappeared after a ship he boarded in Turkey was intercepted by the Russian coastguard and diverted to the Russian-backed breakaway region of Abkhazia. He hasn’t been heard from since. Two Belarusian nationals were briefly detained over the June 2026 fatal shooting of exiled Russian artist and dissident Robert Kuzovkov near Poland’s border with Belarus. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that the incident bore the hallmarks of a political killing.

A shrinking safe zone

Democratic states are no longer safe havens for people fleeing authoritarian rule. On top of failing to do enough to prevent transnational repression on their soil, many are enabling it through their border and immigration systems, as geopolitical calculations and political pressure to curb immigration numbers trump human rights protections.

In June, Germany returned Tajik opposition activist Asadullo Boboev and his 19-year-old son despite a documented risk of arrest. Tajik authorities detained Boboev the moment he landed. He was the fourth activist Germany has deported to face immediate detention in Tajikistan since 2023.

The US government has repeatedly returned Russians to face the authoritarian government they fled. In July 2025, a court in the Russian city of Perm charged opposition activist Leonid Melekhin with ‘justifying terrorism’ immediately after the USA deported him. Weeks later, Russian authorities jailed army deserter Artyom Vovchenko on arrival in Moscow following his deportation from the USA.

US immigration authorities have also deported dozens of detained Iranian asylum seekers after letting Iranian consular officials into detention facilities to help process them. Those deported on chartered flights to a country where they could face the death penalty include Christian converts and women’s rights protesters.

On top of this, the Trump administration’s 2025 dismantling of USAID and freeze on State Department democracy funding cut off money that had helped threatened activists relocate and rebuild their lives abroad, pushing many organisations that support exiles towards financial collapse.

There are, more positively, instances in which courts and governments have held perpetrators to account. UK and US courts convicted those behind the plots against Masih Alinejad and Pouria Zeraati. In June, a UK court convicted a former Border Force officer and a retired Hong Kong police officer of spying on UK-based Hong Kong democracy activists. In March 2025, the USA applied visa bans on current and former Thai officials responsible for or complicit in Thailand’s forced return of Uyghurs to China. These moves offered a welcome break from the tendency of global north democracies to condemn transnational repression without penalising perpetrators.

After Nicaragua stripped hundreds of exiled dissidents of citizenship, several states, including Chile and Spain, immediately stepped up to grant them nationality. But such responses remain the exception. When they offer some protection, host governments tend to concentrate help on a small circle of high-profile figures, leaving most exiles to manage their own security.

Hard-won protections may also be reversible. Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the UK and the USA suspended extradition cooperation with Hong Kong in 2020 when it introduced a draconian national security law. In 2025, however, the UK reversed course, reopening the door to extraditions on a ‘case-by-case basis’. Exiled activists, some with bounties on their heads, condemned this as a betrayal of the roughly 200,000 Hong Kongers who resettled in the UK trusting they’d be protected.

Growing recognition

As the problem has grown, so has its recognition. The European Parliament, the G7 and the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights have all formally acknowledged transnational repression as an assault on human rights and national sovereignty. But recognition hasn’t translated into stronger responses. According to the International Partnership for Human Rights, the European Union’s Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime is poorly suited to tackling transnational repression, as it only applies to serious violations such as killing and torture, while most transnational repression works through subtler means.

Exiled communities have largely filled the gap themselves. Some, such as the Belarusian Solidarity Center in Poland, offer newly arrived activists practical support, including help finding housing, legal orientation and safety planning. Others focus on documenting abuses back home, gathering testimony and evidence that those who’ve stayed can no longer safely collect, as Mexico-based Justicia 11J does for Cuba. Some, including the Hong Kong Democracy Council in Washington, DC, advocate with host governments, pressing for sanctions, visa protections and formal recognition of the threat.

But this work depends on funding that can vanish overnight. The multi-donor Lifeline fund, which once supported embattled civil society organisations, shut down in 2025. And civil society, however well organised, has no power to stop a hostile government’s intelligence services from operating on foreign soil, or to compel governments to act against them. As transnational repression tactics sharpen and intensify, democratic states must live up to their human rights commitments and do everything they can to ensure that exile means safety.

OUR CALLS FOR ACTION

States must end all acts of transnational repression and cooperate fully with investigations and prosecutions.

Democratic states must protect exiles and their families, refrain from deporting or extraditing anyone who faces danger, keep their asylum and immigration systems from being instrumentalised for repression and impose targeted sanctions on those responsible.

Civil society should keep documenting cases, supporting exiled activists and their families and holding host and home governments to account.

For interviews or more information, please contact research@civicus.org

title: AP Source: ICE officer charged with lying to investigators in the shooting of Venezuelan man
description:

The prosecutor was fired on Thursday and is now under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury probe, the person said.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal prosecutors have charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about the events leading up to the shooting of a Venezuelan man during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.

The person was not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on condition of anonymity. The person said Christian Castro, the officer who authorities say shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in January, has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators.

The federal charges follow Castro’s release from jail last week after Texas’ governor refused to immediately sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities, who have charged him separately with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel during the confrontation. But federal prosecutors dropped charges against the men after video evidence showed the officers may have lied about the encounter, and officials opened an investigation.

Earlier this week, a federal prosecutor working on the case told lawyers for Sosa-Celis and other victims that Justice Department officials blocked the prosecutor’s push to bring a more serious civil rights charge against the officer for the shooting, ProPublica reported.

But the person familiar with the investigation disputed the prosecutor’s characterization, saying the probe is continuing and no final decision has been made about whether additional charges will be brought. The prosecutor was fired on Thursday and is now under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury probe, the person said.

An automatic email response from the prosecutor’s Justice Department said he was on leave. Other attempts to reach the prosecutor were not immediately successful.

title: Reports of ICE surge in Indianapolis prompt congressional inquiry - WFYI
description:
Carson, who represents most of Indianapolis and all of Marion County, launched a congressional inquiry seeking the scope and probable cause in the “apparent increased enforcement” in Marion County.
“Those who obstruct ICE operations in Indiana should be arrested and prosecuted,” Banks wrote in a social media post.
“We will not let Indianapolis become Minneapolis.” Indiana’s Republican-controlled state government supports the Trump administration’s expanded immigration enforcement.
“IMPD is not involved in any immigration enforcement operations,” the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department’s Public Information Office said.
Exodus Refugee Immigration, a local support group, spoke out about the recent apparent increase in ICE activity in Marion County.
text:
Reports of stepped up immigration enforcement activity in Indianapolis have drawn sharply divided reactions this week — an immigrant aid group warning of racial profiling at traffic stops, a U.S. senator celebrating the crackdown and city officials insisting they’ve had no role in it. Now, Democrat U.S. Rep. André Carson wants an explanation from federal officials.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has not confirmed an increase in enforcement activity or provided WFYI an official account of its operations in Marion County.

Numerous social media users have posted photos and videos of ICE agents and other officers with the word “police” arresting people around the city. Some officers appeared to be wearing masks. WFYI has not been able to verify the posts.

Carson, who represents most of Indianapolis and all of Marion County, launched a congressional inquiry seeking the scope and probable cause in the “apparent increased enforcement” in Marion County.

Carson sent a letter addressed to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella. “I write to demand information on reports of a surge in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests across Indianapolis, including operations involving masked agents, unmarked vehicles, and a dangerous foot pursuit across multiple lanes of traffic,” he wrote. Carson asked for a reply by Sept. 9.

Carson’s letter seeks “information on any increase in enforcement operations in my district, the authority under which these operations are being conducted, and what safeguards are in place to protect my constituents’ constitutional rights and physical safety,” including the probable cause for the agency’s operations.

Carson also said his office can help constituents with detained family members and can request answers. The office compiled a list of legal resources at carson.house.gov.

U.S. Senator Jim Banks said ICE agents have a constitutional responsibility to deport people who are not in the country lawfully.

“Those who obstruct ICE operations in Indiana should be arrested and prosecuted,” Banks wrote in a social media post. “We will not let Indianapolis become Minneapolis.”

Indiana’s Republican-controlled state government supports the Trump administration’s expanded immigration enforcement. Lawmakers passed Senate Enrolled Act 76, known as the FAIRNESS Act, earlier this year — a law that requires schools, local governments, police departments and sheriff’s offices to follow and work with federal immigration enforcement.

Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith expressed support for ICE. This follows his appearance in a video last month at a private event billed as the nation’s first “mass deportation rally” in Clinton County.

“I proudly support all ICE officers in our state today removing illegal immigrants and helping to keep Hoosiers safe,” he wrote on social media.

ICE responded to a WFYI email seeking details about its activities in Indiana. The agency did not provide any details or answer those questions. But an unidentified spokesperson said ICE works to enforce immigration laws every day in all 50 states.

ICE also provided a list of five people it arrested in Indiana described as “the worst of the worst” in the email, but the agency would not clarify when those people were arrested or detained. In response to questions seeking clarification, the agency provided the administration’s account of how many people had been arrested, deported or left the U.S.

Indianapolis responds

Local officials in Marion County have not been able to provide details and say that they are not involved.

Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett’s office said in a statement that ICE has not communicated with any city or county agency.

“Neither the Mayor’s Office nor any agency within the City-County enterprise has received any communication from federal immigration enforcement authorities regarding current or future operations in Marion County,” Hogsett’s statement said in part.

Indianapolis City-County Council President Maggie Lewis said the council understands the concern and uncertainty the reports of ICE may create for residents and families across our community.

“At this time, we have no information indicating that federal immigration authorities have formally changed their approach or are specifically targeting Indianapolis.”

Indianapolis law enforcement agencies echoed the city leaders’ statements in emails to WFYI.

“IMPD is not involved in any immigration enforcement operations,” the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department’s Public Information Office said. “Our focus remains local public safety and crime reduction.”

“Other than what is being reported in local media, we have no information regarding ongoing ICE investigations. Please refer to DHS for further information,” said Marion County Sheriff’s Office Director of Communications Katie Stanley.

Exodus Refugee Immigration, a local support group, spoke out about the recent apparent increase in ICE activity in Marion County.

“There’s been a rapid increase in ICE activity here in Indy, and in Bloomington,” said Exodus CEO Cole Varga in a video statement posted online. He said that Latino and Haitian residents “are heavily affected right now,” and that immigrants who recently lost Temporary Protected Status and others are primarily being targeted via traffic stops and racial profiling.

The organization urged its clients not to drive right now and is launching a transportation fund with a goal to raise $10,000 to help clients get rides via Uber. It is also seeking volunteers to help with grocery delivery and donations of supplemental food items.

title: Wisconsin ICE arrests hit new high this summer, new data shows
description:
Immigration arrests slowed but remained elevated in July.
Arrests were particularly high in the last week of June, when a team of ICE agents came from Illinois to southeast Wisconsin for what it called a "targeted operation."
From June 26 to June 30, agents arrested and detained around 20 people each day, the data shows.
During that five-day window in Milwaukee in June, ICE arrested 38 people without criminal convictions or pending charges.
The Trump administration also arrested and detained nine people under the age of 18 in Wisconsin, the data shows.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested significantly more people in Wisconsin in June and July than it has in any other month of this administration, according to recently released data.

A Milwaukee Journal Sentinel analysis found that ICE detained and arrested more than 250 people in Wisconsin in June alone, an 82% increase compared to the previous month. Immigration arrests slowed but remained elevated in July.

The rise in arrests comes as part of a national push by the Trump administration to increase immigration enforcement, funneling billions more in funding to ICE to hire more agents.

Arrests were particularly high in the last week of June, when a team of ICE agents came from Illinois to southeast Wisconsin for what it called a "targeted operation." From June 26 to June 30, agents arrested and detained around 20 people each day, the data shows.

The brief operation differed from the quieter, more targeted arrests of people at jails and courthouses that have been more typical in Milwaukee. Instead, video footage captured agents arresting people on the streets by boxing in cars and breaking windows, with some pointing guns.

While the Department of Homeland Security claimed that many of those arrested in the June operation had criminal histories, the data shows that only one-fifth of the people arrested in Milwaukee around that time had convictions or pending criminal charges.

During that five-day window in Milwaukee in June, ICE arrested 38 people without criminal convictions or pending charges. That figure does not include anybody picked up directly from jails or prisons. For comparison, agents arrested an average of three people without criminal records in the same timeframe in July.

The Journal Sentinel based its analysis on data released by the Deportation Data Project, a team of researchers and lawyers at the University of California.

In an email Sept. 2, a spokesperson for DHS said the data is being "cherry picked" by the group. However, the Deportation Data Project obtained the data from DHS itself after winning a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

The data shows that many months with elevated arrest numbers correspond to specific ICE operations, including the June operation in southeast Wisconsin and the "Metro Surge" operation in Minneapolis in December and January.

In addition, arrests of people without criminal records tended to be higher in these months, like in June, when over a quarter of those arrested had no criminal convictions or pending charges.

Overall, Trump's second term has seen an increase in the number of arrests of immigrants without criminal records compared to Biden.

Of those arrested in Wisconsin deemed by ICE to be "convicted criminals," more than 90% are not associated with violent crimes, such as assault and robbery, the data shows.

Instead, the vast majority are classified as "nonviolent crimes," with traffic offenses being by far the most common charge people faced. Other nonviolent offenses include drunken driving, drug trafficking and disorderly conduct.

The Trump administration also arrested and detained nine people under the age of 18 in Wisconsin, the data shows. Of them, the youngest was 4.

DHS said that reflects children being taken into custody along with their parents.

"ICE does not separate families or deport U.S. citizens. Parents are asked if they want to be removed with their children or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates," a DHS spokesperson said.

Darryl Morin, president of advocacy organization Forward Latino, said he is expecting arrests across the country to increase in the coming months as ICE hires more agents.

By and large, Morin said, people understand the need to enforce immigration laws. He said it is the targeting of people without criminal records and those who have work permits or pending immigration cases that is troubling.

"If they were truly taking the worst of the worst, I wouldn't have so many employers calling us, asking for guidance on what they could do to help individuals that worked for them that were lawfully here," Morin said.

Eva Wen is an investigative data reporter. Reach her at qwen@usatodayco.com.

title: ICE arrests hit record highs in Nevada over the summer
description:
Weekly immigration arrests in Nevada hit a record high earlier this summer, according to a Nevada Independent analysis of federal immigration data, even as the Trump administration moves away from the militaristic, high-profile raids seen earlier this year in states such as Minnesota.
In Texas, for example, daily arrests total nearly 400, which is more arrests than Nevada has seen in a single month.
During more than two years of ICE arrests under President Joe Biden, there were higher rates of people with convictions for violent crimes.
Although the most publicized ICE arrests happen in the open, the vast majority of arrests in Nevada happen when a person is in custody, such as at detention centers or local jails.
In contrast to the summer spike in ICE arrests in Nevada, immigration enforcement-related arrests by local law enforcement deputized by ICE were low.
text:
Weekly immigration arrests in Nevada hit a record high earlier this summer, according to a Nevada Independent analysis of federal immigration data, even as the Trump administration moves away from the militaristic, high-profile raids seen earlier this year in states such as Minnesota.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 203 people in Nevada across a two-week span from late June to early July, by far the most people arrested in a two-week period in Nevada on record. This period also saw a significant jump in the percent of people arrested with no criminal record.

One week in June also saw a record number of people arrested in the community, rather than while in custody.

The data confirms anecdotal reports from attorneys and advocates of increasing enforcement activity in Nevada and nationwide. Nevadans for the Common Good, a coalition of faith-based groups and nonprofits, told The Indy in June that seven of its members were detained by ICE during a two-week period that month, including three who were picked up during traffic stops.

The findings are part of the latest release from the Deportation Data Project, an initiative out of the University of California, Berkeley, that publishes data on ICE arrests and detentions accessed through public records requests. This release covers ICE arrest data from mid-March through early August.

While Nevada has so far avoided the large-scale deportation raids seen in states such as California and Minnesota, ICE has still maintained a steady presence in the state, which has one of the highest per capita undocumented populations nationwide, The Indy's prior analyses showed.

"They are looking to have as high numbers of arrests as possible, but with as low a public profile as they can," said Michael Kagan, director of the UNLV Immigration Clinic.

Nevada's arrest numbers still pale in comparison to some other states. In Texas, for example, daily arrests total nearly 400, which is more arrests than Nevada has seen in a single month.

But by Nevada's standards, the latest batch of data shows federal immigration enforcement has not relented.

April, June and July had the three highest number of arrests in Nevada, The Indy found. Arrests had been largely trending downward from July 2025 through February, but they took off again in the spring.

The spike in arrests this summer comes after ICE received more than $35 billion in June through an omnibus immigration package, which will fund the agency through the rest of Trump's presidency. There are subtle signs ICE is looking to expand in the Las Vegas area, such as its recent solicitation to lease parking spaces downtown under a notice labeled "surgeparking."

The agency is also on a hiring spree, with 29,000 employees in June, an increase of about 8,000 from the start of Trump's term, The New York Times reported last week.

Increase in arrests of people with no criminal record

As has been the case through much of Trump's second term, the share of people arrested in Nevada with no criminal record has been steadily increasing.

In the five months covered in the latest data release, 18 percent of arrests were of people with no criminal charges. Under the rest of Trump's second term, that number was 12 percent. At the same time, the percent of people with criminal convictions fell slightly, while the percent with pending charges increased.

Still, these numbers differ significantly from the rest of the country. Under Trump's second term, about 39 percent of people arrested by ICE nationwide had no criminal record, while about 31 percent had previous criminal convictions. The Indy's analysis found.

Even among people with a criminal conviction, many are for nonviolent crimes.

In Nevada, about 8 percent of people's criminal convictions were for violent crimes. That means of the about 5,000 people arrested by ICE in Nevada this year, about 3 percent had a criminal conviction for a violent crime.

During more than two years of ICE arrests under President Joe Biden, there were higher rates of people with convictions for violent crimes.

Where are the arrests happening?

Although the most publicized ICE arrests happen in the open, the vast majority of arrests in Nevada happen when a person is in custody, such as at detention centers or local jails. Under the Trump administration, about 73 percent of ICE arrests happened when a person was already in custody, a slightly higher rate from the latter half of the Biden administration.

However, the tides are slowly turning.

In the latest release of arrest data, more than 30 percent of arrests were "at-large," meaning they happened out in the community. This was about a 25 percent increase from the rest of the Trump administration.

During the week of June 22, 70 arrests happened "at-large," the highest number on record. That week also had the highest number of total arrests.

In contrast to the summer spike in ICE arrests in Nevada, immigration enforcement-related arrests by local law enforcement deputized by ICE were low.

The partnership program, known as 287(g), deputizes law enforcement to carry out immigration enforcement duties within their jails, allowing officers to execute ICE arrest warrants and hold people for longer so ICE can pick them up for long-term detention. Five agencies in Nevada already have partnerships through this program — most notably the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department — and the Nevada Department of Corrections quietly joined the program in July, expanding its ability to coordinate with ICE on immigration arrests.

However, the ICE data shows 24 people have been arrested through the 287(g) program under Trump, making up less than 0.5 percent of all arrests since he took office.

This pales in comparison to other states. Several states with leadership particularly friendly to Trump's immigration policies have seen more than 20 percent of their arrests come through these partnership programs. West Virginia leads the pack at more than 60 percent.

Nevada ranks 34th in share of arrests through the 287(g) program.

text:
Business is better than ever for Karla Navarrete. And she’s not happy about it at all.

She’s an immigration attorney who spends six days a week telling people that they have little chance of staying in Donald Trump’s America.

“It’s become a deportation mill, and my clients have been placed on speeding rockets,” Navarrete, the daughter of a Mexican immigrant, told me at her South Gate office around 8 on a recent Monday morning.

The 42-year-old mother of four had arrived at sunrise to prep for a day of virtual and in-person court hearings and free walk-in consultations. Tchotchkes gifted by grateful clients prettied the pink cabinets and pink walls. Amid statues and posters of the Virgen de Guadalupe was a rosary that a man had made of hardened bread during his months in an immigration detention facility.

On Navarrete’s desk were two Mac laptops and another computer, all logged into immigration courts across the Southland. The private practice she started in 2022 in a small suite now occupies an entire floor and a downstairs reception area, with satellite offices in Chino and downtown Los Angeles.

“Almost none of my clients have a winning case based on current law,” she continued. “’¿Si pasan reforma? [If they pass immigration reform?]’ is their most favorite question. But it’s not just Trump. It’s Stephen Miller, it’s Congress, and it’s becoming the courts.”

A judge called her name. She turned on a heart-shaped computer light, stroked back her long hair and unmuted herself.

“Good morning, your honor,” Navarrete said, her voice barely audible over the air conditioning blasting in her office. Her client, who was grabbed by immigration agents at a car wash last August, was seeking asylum because of the violence endemic in his region of Mexico. The judge was wondering where the man’s paperwork was.

“I’ll give you a few moments,” the judge said. “Make sure it’s complete, counsel. Otherwise, I’ll reject it.”

Navarrete, a San Diego-area native, became an attorney because she has lived through the capriciousness of American immigration law. Her Mexican mother was naturalized thanks to the 1986 amnesty, but her first husband struggled for years to attain legal status.

She flagged down an aide to see what was going on with the file. The court’s uploading system was spotty that morning, the aide said.

Immigration problems still rack Navarrete’s personal life. A member of her extended family faces deportation. Her current husband lost his green card when they moved to a new home to be closer to her job, threatening a long-planned trip to Mexico City.

“He’s going to have to pay a $700 fine and hope he can get a temporary one,” she said before smiling for what would be one of the only times that day. “Otherwise, he’s gonna have to stay here and babysit.”

After a few tense minutes, the judge said he had the client’s file and ordered the man to return in a few months. Navarrete’s other two virtual hearings of the morning ended similarly, with the client ordered back at a later date.

Next up: Zoom calls with clients. Navarrete reveled with one woman over her husband’s release from a detention facility.

She didn’t sugarcoat reality to the next client, whose husband was in immigration detention and had a standing deportation order. (I was able to listen in on sessions with current and prospective clients, provided I didn’t use their names to protect their privacy.)

“We just have to get him out so he can spend as much time together with you,” Navarrete said in Spanish.

“Well, is there a possibility that he could remain?” the woman replied.

“In this moment, no,” Navarrete said.

The woman stayed silent for a good five seconds before saying, “Gracias,” as her voice cracked.

Navarrete, whose biceps are adorned with a tattoo of her mother and one of the Virgen de Guadalupe as a Zapatista rebel, took off her fuchsia blazer to freshen up for a court hearing in Santa Ana. Such trips will soon become more common: She said court officials have told her that almost all hearings will soon be in person.

“They know it’s going to create chaos for immigrants and their lawyers,” Navarrete said, looking at her long acrylic nails, which she gets done every other week as a form of self-care. “But ‘immigration’ now is just a deportation template. It feels fundamentally unfair.”

Navarrete’s life changed last June when she got a phone call while hanging out with her preteen daughter.

Immigration agents had staged a mass raid of Ambiance Apparel in L.A.’s Fashion District. She headed over, finding that friends from UCLA, Loyola Law School and her time working for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights were converging there.

“We were like, ‘What are we going to do? Is this really happening? This, in L.A.?’” she said.

It was the start of a summer of raids that soon went nationwide and have never really ended.

At the time, most of Navarrete’s clients were women applying for a U visa, which offers legal status for crime victims who assist law enforcement in the prosecution of perpetrators. She quickly transitioned to helping people caught up in Trump’s deportation deluge, earning clients through word of mouth as well as through nonprofits such as the CLEAN Carwash Worker Center, which organizes carwasheros across Southern California.

Most of her clients now are middle-aged men, who often choose deportation over the harsh reality of staying in immigration detention indefinitely.

“It’s the younger ones who want to wait it out longer,” she said on the drive down to Santa Ana. An assistant took the wheel of Navarrete’s Range Rover so her boss could catch up on emails, calls and texts.

Family vacations have become limited to weekend getaways, because judges can schedule hearings at any time. Once, Navarrete represented a client virtually from a hotel room, a work jacket over her swimsuit while the rest of her family lounged at the beach.

Her client in Santa Ana had lived in the United States for decades and had a son in the military. Navarrete hoped the judge and the federal government would agree to a hearing on whether the father qualified for parole in place, which offers legal status and a pathway to permanent residency for some immigrants, including parents of active duty service members.

The strategy worked. The judge scheduled a hearing for early next year.

Outside the courthouse, Navarrete listed all the documents her client would need for a chance to stay, as his daughter furiously typed them into a cellphone.

“In another time, this case would’ve been wrapped up in six months,” Navarrete said on the drive back up to South Gate. “Now, everyone’s on the chopping block, and people are becoming desensitized to this if they’re not directly affected. Every [detained immigrant] becomes just another GoFundMe page to ignore.”

Thai food greeted Navarrete at the office — red curry, fried rice, drunken noodles. She ate alongside her employees, who were almost all decked out in black slacks and pink polo shirts bearing her firm’s name and its hummingbird logo.

Jocelyn Xoletl, who joined the office after Navarrete helped a family friend legalize their status, marveled at her boss’ energy.

“Every day I get up and say, ‘How am I so tired?’ and she gets up at 5 a.m. as a wife, a mom and an attorney,” said Xoletl, 23, who plans to attend law school. “She has a ‘do it’ mentality, which is so needed right now.”

“How we’re doing?” Navarrete suddenly called out. “Who we got? Start sending them up.”

A second shift of employees assisted with a parade of people who came in with high hopes and usually left clinging to them after their free consultations.

A Salvadoran woman who had lived in the U.S. since the 1980s held a summons for an immigration hearing while commenting that Navarette looked better than she had in a while.

“I’m doing Pilates now,” Navarrete replied in Spanish. “But Mama, I think they want to arrest you. I can accompany you, but I don’t think it’s to interview you.”

Navarrete kept calm even as the stories she heard grew sadder and sadder. She told a woman that her previous attorney had pursued a habeas petition to get her husband out of immigration detention, when all they needed to do was post bond. It was too late to remedy the error.

“I can’t keep throwing and throwing more money, because I don’t have the money, and I haven’t been able to help him,” the woman said in Spanish, weeping.

When a millennial Latina asked about applying for asylum based on her sexual orientation, Navarrete replied that the Trump administration would likely turn down her claim by pointing out that Mexico hosts Pride parades.

Even the good news came with bad. Navarrete posed for a photo with a client who held an oversized green card to mark his acquisition of the real thing. Then, she told him that his wife would have to spend a few years in Mexico to qualify for permanent residency through him.

“The two of you came happy to celebrate good news,” Navarrete told the quiet couple in Spanish, “and I came to embitter your day.”

Office assistants popped confetti streamers for a man recently released on bond from the Adelanto immigration detention facility, which Navarrete visits at least once a week, after she successfully petitioned a judge. He was still wearing an Adelanto identification bracelet and an ankle monitor to make sure he didn’t venture farther than 75 miles from his home.

Agents had nabbed the Mexico native while he was on a landscaping job. Of the dozen or so other men arrested that day, he told Navarrete, he was one of two who didn’t immediately sign deportation papers.

“So what did your wife make for you when you came back home?” she asked, trying to lighten the mood. His teenage sons stood to the side.

“Mole,” the man said in Spanish. “I missed it so much.”

Her final clients were two parents and their adult son, who were all in danger of being deported. The son had missed an immigration check-in, imperiling his chances of remaining in the U.S.

“I hate to be a realist to you, brother,” Navarrete told the young man, who wore a Dodgers hat and was awaiting the birth of his first child in weeks. “I wish I could give you a response that would allay your worries, but I can’t.”

Around 9 p.m., Navarrete let out a sigh. Another 14-hour day was about to end. She picked up her personal phone to check on her family and grabbed a bag for back-to-school supplies she had ordered from Amazon.

“It was hard today,” Navarrete said. “It was a lot of bad news. No one was a straight shot.”

I asked why she was so blunt with people about their chances.

“I can’t tell them it’s going to be OK. I don’t want to lie: It’s never been this bad,” she said. “I used to call my presentations ‘Know Your Rights’ workshops. Now, they’re just workshops, because there are no rights.”

Navarrete pulled out new V-neck law firm T-shirts for her employees, made by a grateful client.

“As crazy and as chaotic as it can get, every once in awhile, you get a win,” she continued. “And that’s what makes it all worthwhile. It’s gotten harder but more gratifying, because I always wanted to go against ICE, the arch-nemesis of my life.”

Everyone lingered in the parking lot for a few minutes to discuss the week to come. Then, Navarrete remembered her own immigration problem. She and her husband needed to be in Westwood at 7 the next morning to see if he could get a temporary green card.

“What do you think? Will they let my husband get his stamp?” she asked.

He did get it, she told me later. Most of her clients won’t be so lucky.

title: What we're learning from the ground about Immigration Enforcement and a big update to our ...
description:
We have made some major changes to the Immigration Enforcement sections of our Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement: Reporting and Raids.
Why have we rewritten the immigration raids section of the Key Guide?
At the same time, access to legal advice in immigration detention has been recorded at an all-time low.
What has changed in the Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement?
You can read the full Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement: Reporting and Raids here.
text:
We have made some major changes to the Immigration Enforcement sections of our Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement: Reporting and Raids.

The updated guide includes clearer information about voluntary questioning and formal immigration powers, police and Immigration Enforcement working together, warrants and searches, phones and electronic devices, and what people can do during and after an enforcement operation. We have also rewritten the Action Sections to make them easier to use during an enforcement situation based on what we are learning from anti-raids organising and what communities are experiencing on the ground.

Why have we rewritten the immigration raids section of the Key Guide?

Our Public Legal Education team is perhaps a grand name for two people: me, working full-time from Leeds, and Louise, working four days a week in Birmingham, who joined us in May this year. Right to Remain is a tiny organisation, but the work we do, and our mission for migrant justice, are by no means small.

Over the summer, we have been undertaking a huge rewrite of the Toolkit while preparing for yet more changes expected this autumn. A lot of our work is trying to make sense of an immigration and asylum system that changes constantly, work out what those changes mean in practice, and turn that into information people can actually use. It has, quite honestly, felt relentless and infuriating. We are living through the consequences of a Government response to migration that is built on racism and punishment, while the reasons people move, and the harm created by the immigration system itself, are ignored. And the answer, again and again, is more enforcement, more detention and more money lining the pockets of the private companies who deliver it and continue to profit from human suffering.

Having only published our Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement in December 2025, of all the pages that needed updating I had not expected this to suddenly be on the top of my to-do list. But a lot has changed in this short space of time. Immigration enforcement continues to increase (Between January and June 2026, the Home Office carried out 7,270 illegal working visits and made 4,756 arrests – that’s an increase of 31% and 20% compared with the same period in 2025.) There has also been a new policy on illegal working for people living in asylum support, while the government is pushing ahead with plans to significantly expand the immigration detention estate. At the same time, access to legal advice in immigration detention has been recorded at an all-time low.

Learning from a recent immigration raid

Some of these questions came into sharp focus during a recent Immigration Enforcement visit to a late-night hot food takeaway in Leeds.

Eight officers arrived in two unmarked vehicles with a warrant for one named person, who was not there. Officers said they were relying on the warrant, but then questioned other workers about their work and immigration situation, repeatedly demanding information, and questioning why workers were acting nervous, suggesting this was suspicious behaviour. Officers looked through information on workers phones questioning why they had made phone calls and what WhatsApp groups they were in.

Follow-up from Leeds Anti-Raids with the workers also established that the person named on the warrant had valid immigration permission and was complying with their conditions. Eight officers, two vehicles, more than an hour of disruption, frightened workers and invasive questioning, for an operation that ended with nobody being taken. You might be asking the same basic question we were left with: what was all of that for?

For us, this also exposed where ‘know your rights’ messages can become difficult in practice. In a tense and intimidating situation, with officers speaking and acting with seemingly unquestionable authority, it can be hard to work out what is actually happening. You can quickly start to doubt yourself and feel that you have no choice but to comply. If officers have a warrant for one person, what allows them to start questioning somebody else? What changes if the workplace is licensed to serve late-night hot food, where officers may have a separate power to enter without permission? When does a voluntary conversation become a formal immigration examination? Can someone’s understandable fear during a raid be treated as “suspicious” and used to justify further questioning? And what allows officers to take or look through someone’s phone?

This experience reminded us that having legal information is one thing, but being able to use it in a high stakes situation is another. Enforcement situations are frightening, can shift quickly, and officers do not always behave in-line with written policy. Knowledge on its own is only a grain of sand in machinery that runs through everyday life often in ways that are hard to see but reaching into peoples lives in ways that are difficult, and often impossible, to escape. The Toolkit is an important resource, but it is most powerful when it is used through relationships and trust, alongside people rather than simply handed to them.

In Leeds, it was a customer who first raised the alarm in a local alerts group. They knew how to do this because Leeds Anti-Raids had already spent time building relationships and sharing information in the area. The staff also knew who Leeds Anti-Raids were and trusted to take support from them. That trust did not appear in the moment of crisis, it had been built beforehand, and it also made meaningful follow-up possible afterwards.

What has changed in the Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement?

Some of these areas were already covered in the original guide, but we have substantially rewritten and expanded the enforcement sections. You can read the full Key Guide on Immigration Enforcement: Reporting and Raids here.

The main changes include:

Clearer information on voluntary questions, formal examinations and public-space stops

A new section on police and Immigration Enforcement working together

Clearer explanations of warrants, consent, licensed premises and the limits of different powers including examples of a court-issued warrant and AD letter

New section with information on Immigration Officers ability to search phones, electronic devices, PINs and passwords

simpler Action Sections with practical questions people can use in the moment

more on supporting someone during a raid and what to do afterwards, including detention planning and recording what happened

updated community safety guidance, reflecting lessons from anti-raids organising, privacy risks, unmarked vehicles and why more people arriving does not always mean more protection

How raids connect to detention and the wider enforcement system that harms us all

What we are still not seeing in the migration justice sector is a strong, shared narrative that connects raids, enforcement and detention. These systems potentially affect millions of people whose right to live in the UK remains conditional, temporary or unresolved, as well as their families and communities. Our Knowledge is Power session on Detention and Enforcement has noticeably less interest than the other sessions we run on other parts of the asylum system, even as enforcement expands. We have even renamed the session to emphasize that resistance is built in communities, and needs to start before raids and before detention happens.

Raids and detention are not separate systems. Enforcement is often the point where someone is questioned, arrested and taken into detention. We’ll keep saying it, and louder for the people at the back: detention affects all of us. When someone is detained, the impact spreads far beyond them. Families, communities, schools, healthcare services, workplaces and others are left picking up the pieces.

For us, this means resistance to enforcement, from raids and reporting through to detention, removal and deportation, cannot be carried only by the people directly affected, grassroots groups or by organisations already working on detention. We need more people, communities, workers and movements to understand how detention connects to what happens in our streets, homes and workplaces, and to see themselves as part of resisting it.

As Louise and I have picked through line after line of immigration law, despairing at the gaps between what policy says and what we know happens in practice, (interspersed with conversations about our respective sweat rates) this summer’s heat has been its own reminder: climate change will increasingly shape migration and displacement, deepening inequalities already built into these systems. The state’s refusal to care runs through all of it: for why people move, for the conditions people are forced to live through, and for the communities left carrying the consequences.

But look at what happened in Leeds – this shows us how communities hold power. Please don’t underestimate those conversations or small acts of connection. When the scale of what we are facing feels overwhelming and exhausting, and so much around us tells us not to trust each other, these relationships matter. The state does not get to decide how we relate to and show up for one another. This is how we build radical solidarity, practice hope and protect one another.

text:
A judge has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship in the US, after the Supreme Court rejected his previous effort.

Trump signed a more narrow executive order after the high court's ruling, seeking to deny citizenship to children of "alien enemies" and those engaged in "birth tourism".

But Judge Deborah Boardman said this, too, was likely an infringement upon the constitutional right of automatic citizenship conferred to those born in the US.

Boardman issued a preliminary injunction on Wednesday temporarily blocking Trump's order, until a lawsuit brought by immigrant advocacy groups is settled. The administration is likely to appeal.

"The 2026 Executive Order is almost certainly unconstitutional," Boardman said, citing the Supreme Court's ruling on Trump's earlier birthright citizenship effort.

"This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President's most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them."

The lawsuit was brought by a group of immigrant rights groups, including CASA and Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project. They had sued over Trump's previous executive order that sought to end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants.

After the Supreme Court's ruling in June, Trump signed a new, more narrow executive order in August. The order targeted "birth tourism", the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies automatically are citizens.

It is already illegal to travel to the US for the purpose of giving birth, but the latest executive order aimed to enhance regulations and expand enforcement against the practice.

It also aimed to eliminate citizenship for children whose parents are considered "alien enemies", a term the administration defines as those belonging to designated terrorist organisations, including drug cartels.

Under the August executive order, children whose parents work for foreign governments in the US also would have had their citizenship denied.

Government lawyers argued that the Supreme Court's ruling in June upholding birthright citizenship did not preclude other, more narrow options to limit the right.

Exceptions have been allowed in the past, they noted, including for the children of diplomats and alien enemies.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Biden attempting to thwart President Trump's commonsense agenda," a White House spokesperson said on Thursday, according to BBC media partner, CBS News.

"The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."
