title: Two pastors detained, a student dead: Haitians in Ohio turn to faith amid fear of ICE
description:
Asked to speak, she took the microphone at Champion City Church.
After the arrests of two Haitian pastors, Adrien and Julio Dumano, local Haitian leaders put out a call for support.
More than 400 people responded — many of them faith leaders, some traveling from as far as Minnesota and Florida — to stand with Springfield.
Standing alongside the road, visiting faith leaders waved American flags and held signs that said, "Release Pastors Julio and Joubert" and "Jesus loves Haitians."
"We are not powerless," said Louis, one of the Haitian leaders who invited clergy to Springfield this weekend.
text:
Only days after two Haitian pastors were detained by federal immigration agents in Springfield, Ohio, the wife of one of the pastors, Denise Adrien Gedeon, arrived at a Friday (Aug. 28) evening vigil in support of Haitians in the embattled city.

Asked to speak, she took the microphone at Champion City Church. Her voice trembling, eyes closed and hand raised, she began to sing: "We give you all the glory. We worship you our Lord, you are worthy to be praised."

Then she spoke in Haitian Creole about her faith and God, with Viles Dorsainvil, a Haitian community leader and pastor, interpreting. "Despite everything, despite the difficult time, we believe in him, and we believe he will see us through," she said, adding she did not want money or food — just the return of her husband, Joubert Adrien, whom she met singing in a church choir in Haiti in 1999. He was detained Aug. 20.

Gedeon's plea was part of an especially turbulent week in Springfield, Ohio. After the arrests of two Haitian pastors, Adrien and Julio Dumano, local Haitian leaders put out a call for support. More than 400 people responded — many of them faith leaders, some traveling from as far as Minnesota and Florida — to stand with Springfield. Three days after Gedeon's plea, Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian college student, died in what his family is describing as a suicide.

Since the U.S. government removed temporary protected status for Haitians a few weeks ago, the Ohio city has been besieged by daily ICE raids, with over 30 Haitians detained by ICE, according to the Haitian Support Center, a nonprofit that assists Haitian nationals in Springfield. The organization estimates that ICE has outfitted more than 100 people with ankle monitors to track their whereabouts.

With about 10,000 Haitians living in the city of 58,000, many have been hiding out in their homes, fearing detainment. A small contingent of local Haitian community leaders, several pastors themselves, braved Friday's vigil. Many Haitian churches sat empty Sunday morning.

During the weekend, hundreds of volunteers — Baptists, Unitarian Universalists, Mennonites, Quakers and others — packed food boxes for Haitians in hiding, held phone drives asking elected officials to release the pastors and stood outside Haitian churches on Sunday morning to advocate for Haitians' right to worship without fear.

That fear has been fueled by the flurry of rapid ICE raids happening throughout the city. Around 9 a.m. on Aug. 20, Gedeon said that she and her husband, Adrien, were riding in a car with Adrien's cousin and his wife. They had just pulled out of a gas station when a car sped in front of them and slammed on the brakes. Four other cars surrounded their vehicle.

"At that time, I kept saying, ‘Please God, let us go, free us, please God, let us go,'" Gedeon recalled, speaking through an interpreter. Several masked officers she identified as ICE agents approached the vehicle and asked to see IDs and work permits, she said. The officers handcuffed the two men. Gedeon, who cried out to her husband before he was taken away, said she hasn't seen him since.

A father of two living in the U.S. for five years, Adrien is the Haitian ministry pastor at High Street Church, a Nazarene congregation in Springfield. Local advocates say he has no criminal history and no final order of removal. The couple had temporary protected status and have pending asylum cases, according to Gedeon.

Speaking to RNS on the back steps of High Street Church, head Pastor Marty Dennis explained that Adrien was part of a group of Haitians who visited his church four years ago seeking a place to worship in Haitian Creole. What began as 15 Haitians worshipping in a living room grew to over 100 people meeting in the church gymnasium, while Dennis' congregation held worship in their sanctuary.

Now the gym is empty. The Haitian congregants are worshipping remotely while Adrien is held in Butler County Jail, about an hour from Springfield. Even in prison, Dennis and Gedeon said, Adrien is ministering to those around him. "He loves God more than life itself," said Dennis. "I couldn't imagine doing life without him."

Gedeon, with the loss of her work permit, now stays at home, caring for their two kids, ages 7 and 14, alone. Last week, their youngest celebrated her seventh birthday without her father. But she said she leans on her faith in God, saying, "Maybe this happened for good reason, and the good reason was for him to go in that detention center, preach to people, be close to people, and give them hope."

Michaelle Louis, a Haitian community organizer with Undivided — one of the several faith groups behind the week's gathering of faith leaders — said ICE is deliberately detaining men — "the head of the family." The idea is, she said, "if they deport the husband, the rest of the family is going to follow."

Carl Ruby, pastor of Central Christian Church and founder of G92, a nonprofit organization that advocates for immigrants, said he learned in meetings with regional and national ICE leaders that their aim is to make living in the U.S. unbearable for Haitians.

"I was surprised how candid they were," said Ruby. "They said … ‘We're going to make life as miserable as possible.'"

Though Springfield doesn't have the largest Haitian population in the U.S., pro-immigrant organizers say their city has been a political target since then-candidate Donald Trump and his running mate, J.D. Vance, spread falsehoods about the city's Haitians eating pets in the run-up to the 2024 presidential election. Nearly two years later, Haitians in Springfield said the ankle monitors, which many compared to slave shackles, are part of a Springfield-specific ICE experiment.

On Monday, 20-year-old Pierre Damas Bel, a pre-med student and soccer player at Wright State University, was fatally struck by a tractor-trailer. Bel's family is describing his death as a suicide. Ohio State Highway Patrol called it "an open investigation."

In a statement written by Bel's father after his son's death, he said his son had taken two trips to Cincinnati to plead with officers to remove his ankle monitor, which was visible when he played soccer. "After my son was outfitted with this ankle monitor, he felt like he was treated like an animal," he wrote. The statement says Bel's classmates bullied him because of the monitor.

A spokesperson for Wright State University said the university was "heartbroken" about the death of Bel. The university has "no confirmed information regarding complaints or investigations into bullying related to the student," the spokesperson said in a statement, adding that "we remain dedicated to providing a campus community where every student feels safe, supported, included and welcomed."

Ruby, who was with Bel's parents Monday night, said he has seen "the extremes" in recent weeks.

"I believe in a good God who will eventually make all things right, who will punish evil and restore justice, but living in the here and now is really hard," he said. One day he gathered with hundreds to protest ICE's immigration policy. The next day, he said, he listened to "the sobs and screams" of Bel's parents.

"We need a revival of the spirit of the prophets where people of faith demand justice in their government and in their churches," he said.

On Sunday morning, dozens of clergy stood outside First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield, one of the city's largest Haitian congregations and home to Pastor Julio Dumano, an assistant pastor at the church who was detained on Aug. 25. The whereabouts of Dumano, who was described by fellow clergy as a "godly man," are currently unknown.

Standing alongside the road, visiting faith leaders waved American flags and held signs that said, "Release Pastors Julio and Joubert" and "Jesus loves Haitians."

Inside, nearly 40 volunteers and faith leaders sat in chairs alongside Haitian congregants, singing "How Great Thou Art" in Haitian Creole and in English. Though the once-packed church had only a few-dozen Haitian members that Sunday, their enthusiasm wasn't diminished. The congregants, wearing suits, dresses and heels in bright colors, danced in worship and welcomed their visitors with enthusiasm.

"Thank you so much for coming," Pastor Reginald Silencieux said warmly from the podium. "When I see your presence, it's very encouraging. When Haitian people see you, they can see Jesus is alive. Amen?"

Hours later, over 400 people made their way to City Hall, where they shared an outdoor potluck, sang "We Shall Overcome" and heard remarks from local leaders. Speakers made three demands of ICE, the Department of Homeland Security and elected officials: release the pastors, stop outfitting Haitians with ankle monitors and stop "treating them inhumanely because of their nationality and the color of their skin."

"We're making these demands in the name of Christ," Ruby said at the rally.

At the conclusion of Sunday's event, Haitian pastor Bernadette Dor-Dominique invited attendees to march seven times around City Hall. She explained that the "Jericho march" was a reference to the biblical book of Joshua, which says God tore down the walls of Jericho after the Israelites marched around the city for seven days.

"It is a symbolic act of faith, unity, perseverance and trust in God when the situation appears impossible," said Dor-Dominique. "We are walking against fear and division, standing together as one community."

Since Springfield's Haitian population became national news during the 2024 campaign, the city has endured bomb threats, neo-Nazi rallies and now an ICE surge. But pro-immigrant advocates, like Louis, say the city's story remains one of resilience and faith.

"We are not powerless," said Louis, one of the Haitian leaders who invited clergy to Springfield this weekend.

Ruby, for his part, said he was "encouraged" by the number of volunteers who showed up Sunday, but "until the entire church practices a faith that looks like Jesus, we have a lot of work to do."

text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. — Mitchell Best, 43, was sentenced to 60 years in federal prison for producing child sexual abuse material depicting a child under the age of five. Best was indicted July 2, 2024, on five counts of production of child sexual abuse material, one count of distribution of child sexual abuse material and one count of possession of child sexual abuse material. He pleaded guilty Feb. 18, 2026, to two production counts and was sentenced to two consecutive 30-year federal prison terms. ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations conducted the probe.

Best was also sentenced in December 2024 to 30 years in state prison for rape. The judge in the case ordered 10 years of Best’s federal sentence to run concurrently with his state sentence; Best then will serve his remaining 50 years.

“Our investigation and the sentence for these heinous crimes reaffirms HSI’s commitment to identifying and bringing those who exploit our most vulnerable to justice,” said acting HSI New Orleans Special Agent in Charge Matt Wright. “This outcome was only possible through the seamless collaboration between our special agents, the Arkansas State Police and the Cabot Police Department. We will continue to leverage every resource at our disposal to investigate these crimes and work alongside our partners to protect children from such predators."

On April 2, 2024, HSI and officers from the Cabot Police Department executed a search warrant at Best’s home. Agents found multiple files of child sexual abuse material, including images and videos that depicted Best sexually assaulting a young child, during a forensic examination of his phone.

The investigation was conducted by HSI with assistance from the Arkansas State Police and the Cabot Police Department. This case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas Kristin Bryant.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse.

If you have information about child exploitation or related crimes, call the ICE Tip Line at 866-DHS-2-ICE (866-347-2423).

The suit seeks a judicial order limiting these and other practices, including conducting immigration enforcement operations from “sensitive” areas such as schools, courthouses and hospitals, and limiting the use of “biometric” scanning of fingerprints and other personal information.

text:
With the anniversary of Operation Midway Blitz less than a week away, the militarized tactics of immigration agents that roiled Chicago last fall were once again front and center in federal court on Wednesday as a judge weighs the merits of a lawsuit alleging the Trump administration’s policies are unconstitutional.

But U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis, who last November issued a landmark preliminary injunction limiting the use of force by immigration agents, seemed more skeptical this time around about her ability to police the Justice Department’s enforcement of immigration laws, particularly in light of an appellate court ruling that she’d overstepped her authority.

“Clearly under the separation of powers, I cannot manage the Executive Branch,” Ellis told the parties during the nearly four hours of arguments. “I think I’d said that before, but I’ve been told it again.”

Ellis harked back to her dramatic decision in a lawsuit brought by the Chicago Headline Club to force then-Border Patrol Cmdr. Greg Bovino, who headed the Midway Blitz operation, to come to court and explain why her orders limiting tear gas and other uses of force on protesters were obviously not being followed.

Ellis said she thought at the time it was well within her role as a judge. But the 7th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals later overruled her, calling it a “constitutionally suspect” violation of the separation of powers.

“I certainly thought that having Mr. Bovino come into court and…demonstrate ‘this is how I complied with this order’ was a way of enforcing an order that I had the right to make,” Ellis said. “There was difference of opinion on whether that violated the separation of powers, and I think that is illustrative of how tricky that can be.”

The plaintiffs have alleged the Justice Department’s tactics were part of a campaign to coerce Illinois and Chicago to abandon sanctuary policies protecting immigrants, in violation of the Tenth Amendment.

But Ellis said she’s “a little hesitant to wade into” drawing the line between law enforcement and coercion. “At what point do I step out of my lane?” she said.

The judge’s comments came as she weighs the government’s motion to dismiss a lawsuit filed jointly by the Illinois Attorney General’s Office and city of Chicago in January alleging a broad swath of illegal actions during the Trump administration’s controversial deportation campaign.

The 103-page lawsuit — which was filed after the Chicago Headline Club case was dismissed — alleged immigration agents acted more like an occupying military force than law enforcement during Midway Blitz, terrorizing neighborhoods with “roving patrols,” illegally switching out license plates, randomly stopping people to question them about their citizenship, and making warrantless arrests.

The suit seeks a judicial order limiting these and other practices, including conducting immigration enforcement operations from “sensitive” areas such as schools, courthouses and hospitals, and limiting the use of “biometric” scanning of fingerprints and other personal information.

Justice Department lawyers argue that the plaintiffs lack standing on almost every count, pointing out Operation Midway Blitz was long over by the time the lawsuit was filed and there was no plausible or imminent threat of harm to citizens.

The government’s motion to dismiss also argued that there had been no showing that any “core” activities of the state or city were disrupted due to the immigration enforcement tactics — another way in which the plaintiffs have alleged ongoing harm.

At the outset of Wednesday’s hearing, Ellis questioned attorney Paul Berks, who represents Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office, the potential harm to Illinois citizens going forward, since the surge of agents ended months ago and it would be mere speculation to say it’s going to return.

“If we’re looking at sort of past is prologue, it seems as though this surge and enforcement happens in one area, and then moves on to another and another and another, without necessarily returning,” Ellis said, noting that after leaving Chicago, agents landed in North Carolina and Minnesota. “So this is where I’m struggling on standing. I can’t really look backwards, necessarily. I have to have some evidence that there is going to be imminent harm in the future.”

Berks said that enhanced immigration enforcement continues in and around Chicago to this day, including increased arrests at courthouses and other co-called “sensitive locations.”

He also cited the administration’s own statements that they were not done with Chicago. Among them: a call by Trump himself on Truth Social for immigration officials “to do all in their power” to effect “the single largest Mass Deportation Program in History” in Democratic power centers like Chicago.

“The motivation is there,” Berks said. “The policies are still in place. The threats have been made…The fact that they haven’t returned to Chicago yet is not evidence that they’re not going to return to Chicago.”

Ellis said she’d rule on the motion to dismiss at the next hearing Nov. 17.

The lawsuit is one of several that are still pending at the Dirksen U.S. Courthouse nearly a year after Operation Midway Blitz began in earnest on Sept. 8, 2025, a roughly two-month surge that led to nearly daily clashes in the streets between protesters and heavily armed agents, who often used tear gas, pepper spray balls, and rubber bullets on crowds.

In October, Ellis held a marathon hearing in the case brought by the Chicago Headline Club before issuing a landmark preliminary injunction limiting such practices. She found in her scathing opinion that not only had agents used inappropriate force, but that immigration leaders, including Bovino, had lied about it under oath.

But Ellis’ injunction was later stayed by the 7th Circuit, and the plaintiffs moved to dismiss the suit without prejudice as a tactical maneuver, which the judge granted.

In March, a 7th Circuit panel voted 2-1 to order what’s known as “vacatur,” which essentially treated Ellis’ preliminary injunction ruling as though it never existed. In the 15-page majority opinion, the judges wrote that Ellis, “working on a highly compressed timeline … granted an overbroad, constitutionally suspect injunction.”

The majority was particularly critical of Ellis for dismissing the lawsuit “without prejudice” even though the parties didn’t ask for it, leaving the door open for plaintiffs to refile the case at some point down the road.

By then, Ellis had already granted a request from lawyers for Illinois and Chicago to preside over their suit — over the strenuous objection of the Justice Department.

Ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, the plaintiffs filed a motion for new discovery into ongoing immigration enforcement efforts in the Chicago area, including information from the past three months about deployment of tear gas, enforcement actions at courthouses and other sensitive locations, warrantless arrests, and “misuse of license plates,” court records show.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio —

A Wright State University student's death by suicide is a mournful reality for the university and for Springfield's Haitian community.

Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old first-year student at Wright State, died on Monday. His family said he was overwhelmed by bullying and shame after immigration agents placed an ankle monitor on him in July.

Bel, an honor roll athlete, had been recruited to play soccer at Wittenberg University but lost his roster spot after receiving the monitor.

"He felt so humiliated," said Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield. "The monitor had just stopped everything."

Despite the setback, Bel enrolled at Wright State to continue his education and pursue his dream of becoming a doctor.

Wright State University President Sue Edwards expressed sorrow over Bel's death, saying, "We are heartbroken by this devastating loss. Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community. The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time."

Even before Bel's death, frustration over the use of ankle monitors had been growing in Springfield's Haitian community, where many have lost their temporary protected status and live in fear of ICE agents. On Friday, faith leaders and Springfield NAACP President Denise Williams rallied for change.

"Unshackle Springfield. Unshackle Springfield," Williams said.

Bel's father said his son died after throwing himself in front of a semi-truck on Interstate 70, overwhelmed by taunts from classmates about the ankle monitor.

"It was devastating news for us," Dorsainvil said.

Dorsainvil hopes Bel's death will lead to policy changes in Washington. "I am calling upon the administration all the time, upon the policymakers to review the policies, because behind them are real human lives. If they can do that, I think that it would be good for the country," he said.

Professors and students at Wright State and residents in Springfield are now navigating the grieving process. Wright State has made counseling available for students, while the Haitian Support Network is planning a memorial for Bel next week.

The investigation into Bel's death remains open. Meanwhile, Dorsainvil is working with a local mental health expert to organize group sessions for young Haitians affected by the tragedy.

The DOJ said states not currently compliant with the reporting requirements will not lose federal funding that has already been allocated, but future dollars would be jeopardized should state agencies refuse to report undocumented immigrants.

text:
The Justice Department sanctioned a powerful new legal tool the Trump administration can use to compel states to assist with the White House’s crackdown on immigration.

The Tuesday opinion by the Office of Legal Counsel sets a framework for the federal government to revoke future welfare grants from states that refuse to report immigrants that did not enter the nation lawfully — another example of the administration threatening to revoke federal funding to force states to provide more data and information about the immigrants who live there.

Funding for federal social services, like Social Security and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, have largely been dispensed at the discretion of the states since Congress overhauled the national welfare system in 1996. That revamp narrowed certain state reporting requirements in an effort to prevent noncitizens from taking welfare benefits. Previous administrations have agreed that the reporting burden falls only on the specific state agencies that dispense those funds.

The Office of Legal Counsel, which provides legal guidance to the executive branch, reversed that precedent this week.

Trending

Dusting off the decades-old, Clinton-era welfare law, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock concluded in his 19-page opinion that the previous reporting requirements were too “narrow.”

Specifically, Craddock asserts that all agencies in a state that receives welfare grants — which includes every state in the union, as well as the District of Columbia and U.S. territories — must now report immigrants they believe illegally came to the country.

The office’s announcement relies on a revamped interpretation of the word “state” under the 1996 law, retooling it to encompass “all component agencies,” not just the specific agency administering federal benefits.

“The mandatory reporting obligations … thus apply to all agencies within a state that participates in the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Supplemental Security Income programs subject to those requirements,” Craddock wrote.

The DOJ said states not currently compliant with the reporting requirements will not lose federal funding that has already been allocated, but future dollars would be jeopardized should state agencies refuse to report undocumented immigrants.

“States remain free to reevaluate their participation in TANF or SSI going forward in view of today’s opinion,” Craddock wrote.

Trump has frequently attempted to withhold federal dollars as a way to ensure so-called sanctuary states and jurisdictions comply with his mass-deportation agenda, but federal judges have consistently ruled against him. More than a dozen states and D.C. have enacted policies aimed at restricting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. It is unclear how the new federal precedent will clash with those state-level mandates, though some may choose to sue the administration over its new directive.

Filed against the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche, the suit contends they are interfering with the right of individual states to conduct free and fair elections.

text:
LOS ANGELES — The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration on Wednesday, alleging the federal government is illegally targeting non-U.S. born citizens to prevent them from exercising their legal right to vote.

Filed against the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche, the suit contends they are interfering with the right of individual states to conduct free and fair elections.

“Naturalized citizens are Americans,” CHIRLA executive director Angelica Salas said at a news conference announcing the lawsuit in downtown Los Angeles on Wednesday. “They took the oath. They earned their citizenship, and they have the same rights as every other American citizen.”

CHIRLA director of organizing and naturalized U.S. citizen, Pedro Trujillo, is also a plaintiff in the lawsuit “because I do not want this federal administration to get away with their attempts at voter intimidation or even worse: creating second-class citizenship where naturalized citizens are not given the rights they have earned,” he said.

Trujillo was brought to the United States by his parents when he was six years old, attended public school, graduated from a state university and applied for, and became, a U.S. citizen after 20 years of being undocumented, he said.

The lawsuit is one of several that has been filed against the Trump administration after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March “Ensuring Citizenship and Integrity in Federal Elections,” which directed the Department of Homeland Security, in partnership with the Social Security Administration, to develop an approved list of absentee voters.

After California and several other states refused to hand over their voter rolls, the Department of Justice sent letters to state election officials in July saying they would be criminally prosecuted if they knowingly retained noncitizens on their rolls, while the Department of Homeland Security said it would withhold Federal Emergency Management Agency funds from states that hadn’t used a DHS system to verify the citizenship of individuals on their voter rolls.

Filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the CHIRLA complaint centers on a letter the Trump administration sent to California officials alleging that more than 190,000 non-citizens are registered to vote in the state.

“Methodology for arriving at this figure has never been provided, and it is almost certainly widely incorrect,” the complaint says.

UCLA Voting Rights Projects Senior Data Scientist Michael Rios said at Wednesday’s news conference that efforts to compare databases, such as the federal government is seeking to do with state voter files, are problematic.

“Names can be misspelled, they can be shortened, they change after marriage, they can be entered differently between databases… There could be issues of capitalization, punctuation and spacing,” Rios said.

“Unless databases have a unique identifier to merge them by, a similar name, birthdate, or address cannot establish that two records represent the same person,” he added. “That’s why you have to extremely careful in methodologies and validation efforts before drawing conclusions.”

The CHIRLA lawsuit is asking the court to declare the Trump administration’s voter list matching unconstitutional and unlawful and to stop the practice.

“DHS is laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens,” a DHS spokesperson told Spectrum News.

“We have repeatedly demonstrated that illegal aliens can and do vote in our elections,” the spokesperson added. “Under President Trump, Homeland Security Investigations is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens, and only American citizens, are electing American leaders.”

Noncitizen voting in any state is “extremely small,” according to the Center for Election Innovation & Research, which found that “claims about possible noncitizen registrations and voting allege vanishingly small numbers. Even the largest claims (which are the most likely to be severe overestimates) never allege numbers that are more than roughly one-tenth of one percent of the number of active registered voters in the state.”

title: Congressman Brad Sherman Statement on Trump Administration Deal Opening the Door to ...
description:
I am profoundly disturbed by the path this agreement creates for a nuclear-armed Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia is in a volatile region that has seen the collapse of many dictatorships that were thought to be stable.
Now, the Trump Administration is green-lighting an uncontrolled nuclear program for Saudi Arabia.
It was the policy of the first Trump Administration that a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia needed to include the Gold Standard and Additional Protocol provisions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio recognized the need for these safeguards years ago when he joined me in introducing the Saudi Nuclear Nonproliferation Act in 2016, and I applaud Senator Kennedy (R-LA) for registering his opposition to this no-safeguards Saudi nuclear deal last month.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman Brad Sherman (CA-32), senior member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, issued the following statement after reviewing the proposed U.S.-Saudi Arabia Section 123 Agreement for peaceful nuclear cooperation submitted to Congress by the Trump Administration:

“I have read the proposed 123 Agreement that the Trump Administration has sent to Congress, both the unclassified and classified portions. The classified portion of the Agreement includes a blank page labeled “to be filled in later.” Clearly the Trump Administration has not submitted the Agreement for review as required by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, which requires that Congress see the whole agreement.

I am profoundly disturbed by the path this agreement creates for a nuclear-armed Saudi Arabia.

This deal claims to facilitate peaceful nuclear technology for Saudi Arabia but intentionally excludes the very safeguards that determine whether or not a country with nuclear technology can use it to build nuclear weapons: the Gold Standard and Additional Protocol. Not only that, but this agreement explicitly allows uranium enrichment on Saudi soil under certain conditions. And only President Trump, not the Congress, will determine if those vague conditions have been met.

Crown Prince Mohammad Bin Salman has been clear about his intentions to pursue a nuclear weapon, and Saudi Arabia has already shown a willingness to advance down that path covertly by standing up an undeclared, Chinese-backed yellowcake-extraction facility just a few years ago.

Saudi Arabia is in a volatile region that has seen the collapse of many dictatorships that were thought to be stable. It was the United States that provided preliminary nuclear technology to Iran through the Atoms for Peace program when it was ruled by a friendly, pro-Western monarch – and all of the technology in the hands of the Shah in 1978 fell into the hands of the Ayatollah in 1979.

Today, we are fighting a war designed to prevent Iran from having an uncontrolled nuclear program. Now, the Trump Administration is green-lighting an uncontrolled nuclear program for Saudi Arabia. While the current Saudi government is far less problematic than the one in Tehran, no one knows who will be in power in Riyadh ten years from now. This region has seen the collapse of many dictatorships that were thought to be stable, and this deal gambles the nuclear security of the United States and the world on the very weak assumption that pro-Western leaders will continue to head Saudi Arabia in the decades to come.

A Saudi nuclear bomb would shred the nonproliferation regime of the last half century. Once Saudi Arabia has an uncontrolled nuclear program with America’s blessing, Egypt, Turkey, and perhaps South Korea and Brazil will not be far behind.

This should not be a Democratic or Republican issue – this is about American national security, and the United States’ longstanding bipartisan commitments to non-proliferation. It was the policy of the first Trump Administration that a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia needed to include the Gold Standard and Additional Protocol provisions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recognized the need for these safeguards years ago when he joined me in introducing the Saudi Nuclear Nonproliferation Act in 2016, and I applaud Senator Kennedy (R-LA) for registering his opposition to this no-safeguards Saudi nuclear deal last month. Members of Congress – Republican and Democrat alike – must reject this deal with a Joint Resolution of Disapproval until the necessary safeguards are included.”

description:
A graveyard of living people, that's how Lorenzo described Camp East Montana, the ICE detention facility where guards denied him sunlight and fresh air for a full month.
I have undocumented neighbors in San Jose who have lived there for more than two decades.
It turned out his friend, Norm, had been taken with his family from their home on Fifth Street in San Jose and incarcerated in Heart Mountain, Wyoming.
That young boy returned to San Jose and grew up.
We must defend human dignity; we must uphold our Constitution; and we must stop digging graveyards for the living.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Sam Liccardo (CA-16) took to the House Floor to condemn Immigrations and Custom Enforcement (ICE) for their role in the deaths of 52 people in their custody since President Donald Trump took office.

“Fifty-two people have died in ICE custody since Donald Trump took office, mothers and fathers, brothers and sisters, daughters and sons, every one someone's child and every one a child of God,” said Liccardo. “Someone loves us, someone mourns us, and when we die, grief takes part of them with us. My heart aches for the families who never got the chance to say goodbye, who never held their loved ones' hand before they died alone behind barbed wire and concrete.”

His somber speech ended with a moment of gratitude for the cities and localities for using local zoning laws to mitigate the expansion of ICE detention facilities and protect the health and safety of our communities. Liccardo’s office created a toolkit to help communities enact ordinances, and so far, the City of San José, San Mateo County, and Napa County have taken a step toward advancing such ordinances.

Read Liccardo’s full remarks below or watch on YouTube. A downloadable version is available for media distribution here.

Floor Remarks:

I'd like to thank Representative Torres for her leadership. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

A graveyard of living people, that's how Lorenzo described Camp East Montana, the ICE detention facility where guards denied him sunlight and fresh air for a full month. Lorenzo persevered. 52 others would never feel the sun upon their face again. 52 people have died in ICE custody since Donald Trump took office, mothers and fathers, brothers and sisters, daughters and sons, every one someone's child and every one a child of God. Someone loves us, someone mourns us, and when we die, grief takes part of them with us. My heart aches for the families who never got the chance to say goodbye, who never held their loved ones' hand before they died alone behind barbed wire and concrete.

I have undocumented neighbors in San Jose who have lived there for more than two decades. They have built lives there. They have built families there. Some coach for youth sports teams. Others volunteer at their church. Several have built businesses, employing U.S. citizens, and all have built our community.

This is not the first time our country has put the most ambitious of our dreamers and doers behind bars. In 1942, my father came home, telling my grandfather that his friend was missing from their weekly pickup baseball game. It turned out his friend, Norm, had been taken with his family from their home on Fifth Street in San Jose and incarcerated in Heart Mountain, Wyoming. Norm was a Japanese American. That young boy returned to San Jose and grew up. And decades later, I had the honor of working for him as his intern. His name is Norm Minneta, and he served in this Congress for two decades. But the incarceration of 120,000 Japanese Americans left an indelible stain on our country.

The last of those who endured it still walk among us, and the ghosts of those who did not endure it still haunt our national conscience. So history will harshly also judge us for the abuse, for the abuse of an inhuman treatment of our undocumented neighbors. Too many of us have declined to speak out, or perhaps only when ICE’s chaotic cruelty takes the life of an American citizen, as in Minneapolis. Yet the deaths in our DHS detention centers continue unabated, accompanied only by the incriminating silence of the quietly complicit.

I'm proud that in my own Bay Area region, San Mateo County, the City of San Jose, the County of Santa Clara, and the County of Napa have all taken steps to obstruct the construction of new detention centers in our communities. We're helping them and others with a toolkit that includes a model ordinance, but local leaders should never have to fight this battle alone. Congress must act. We must defend human dignity; we must uphold our Constitution; and we must stop digging graveyards for the living.

text:
An 33-year-old woman originally from Belarus is asking a court to order her release from immigration detention, claiming she has gone months in an ICE detention center without adequate lifesaving medicine.

Attorneys for Katsiaryna Bartko, who is seeking asylum after entering the U.S. in 2022, on Friday will ask a Kansas federal district court to order her to be released for supervised medical treatment while her immigration case is pending.

Bartko entered the U.S. on a student visa to avoid political persecution over her vocal opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. ICE officials said her student status was terminated in March 2023.

According to court documents, she had applied for asylum the previous month in February 2023.

Bartko was detained by ICE in Florida in June 2026, and taken to the Miramar ICE field office after local charges were dropped for a domestic battery charge.

According to a statement from ICE, "Local law enforcement arrested Katsiaryna Bartko, a criminal illegal alien from Belarus, for battery domestic violence. ICE lodged an immigration detainer on May 6, 2026. Since Florida cooperates, this criminal illegal alien was turned over to ICE."

Bartko's partner, Dmitry Shyshov, said the incident was the result of a disturbance complaint at a party that the two attended. According to the Miami-Dade County court clerk's office, these charges were dropped.

"Her case was dismissed both by the judge and the prosecutor of Miami-Dade, and they pick her up 48 hours after the case was dismissed," Shyshov said. "I was literally spending nights near this field office just because I was so concerned about her health."

Bartko was also charged with disorderly intoxication in 2025, but prosecution was not pursued after she successfully completion a diversion program in June, according to ABC News' review of criminal records.

Bartko reports a past medical history of thyroid cancer and said she requires two pills a day to survive, according to court documents filed on her behalf. She says the pills help regulate critical hormones in her body following treatment for thyroid cancer.

Shyshov claims that while in detention, Bartko has not consistently received her medications, occasionally going without them for days at a time.

If she misses doses, she could slip into severe hormone deficiency and a myxedema coma, with a reported mortality of 25-60%, according to court documents.

"She contends that repeated failures, objective deterioration, and the medical evidence establish that this custody arrangement cannot safely preserve a life sustaining regimen," court documents said.

The documents also say Bartko was taken to an emergency room three separate times in four days during her early detention, including initially with critically low levels of calcium.

"She is non-criminal. She is living here in Miami. We have, like, everything here in Miami, so she'll be easily released," Shyshov said. "But they took her, they transferred her to Kansas."

Shyshov said Bartko, in phone calls from the detention center, described repeated instances of allegedly improper medical care.

"She was without her medications, she faced acute hand symptom, and she came to them and asking, 'Can you call me a doctor?' They said, 'Write a sick note.' She said, 'How? How can I do it?' Shyshov recounted. "They said, 'We don't care.'"

In a statement, a Department of Homeland Security representative said Bartko is "actively receiving proper medical care," adding that ICE is "working with the hospital to ensure that Bartko is covered."

"This includes medical, dental, and mental health intake screening within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arrival at a facility, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care," the statement said.

"This is the best healthcare many aliens have received in their entire lives," said the statement.

Medical records from Bartko's detention provided by Shyshov and reviewed by ABC News suggest she may not have been taking sufficient medication for her condition.

The records show TSH levels were observed to steadily increase to high levels over Bartko's time in custody. TSH stands for thyroid stimulating hormone and levels that are too high or too low may be a sign of a thyroid problem, according to the National Library of Medicine.

Dr. Sarah Raza, a double board-certified physician in vascular and interventional radiology for the Physicians for Human Rights Asylum Network, provided her medical opinion in court documents.

"Ms. Bartko remains at foreseeable risk of serious complications from severe thyroid-hormone under-replacement unless effective replacement therapy and prompt specialist-directed monitoring are established," Raza said. "Placement in any setting that cannot reliably provide, document, and promptly adjust this essential therapy remains medically unsafe."

When asked about these claims, Ryan Gustin, a senior public affairs officer for CoreCivic, the company contracted to operate the detention center, said Bartko is "being regularly monitored by facility medical staff, with all known medical issues being addressed."

"Our onsite health services team at MRRC, as with every facility where we provide medical care, takes seriously their role and responsibility to provide high-quality healthcare, available 24/7, to the individuals in our care," Gustin said.

Shyshov said he constantly worries that Bartko's health will deteriorate silently.

"There will be no screaming, no asking for help, nothing -- just because she will have the throat spasm and she cannot scream in the case of hypocalcemia," Shyshov said. "If she will die in the myxedema coma, it will also happen in a heartbeat."

"You can imagine how terrified I am right now when I'm not hearing from her for hours already" he said.

Regarding Friday's court date, at which Bartko's attorneys will argue for her release, Shyshov said, "It's challenging, but I have no other options except fighting for her."

ENRC brought a civil claim against its former lawyers in 2017 and the SFO in 2019. We are confident that the SFO’s wrongdoing between 2011 and 2013 could never happen again.

The SFO is a fundamentally different organisation. We have overhauled how we operate with stronger governance, independent oversight and clearer safeguards.

Details of the SFO’s budget and expenditure are published in our annual report and accounts.

text:
The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York on September 1, 2026, handed down a significant decision in Rourke-Rodriguez et al. v. U.S. Department of Education, granting summary judgment to the plaintiffs – members of New York's Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe – and striking down a U.S. Department of Education (ED) policy that required American Indian students born in Canada, known as Jay Treaty students, to obtain immigration documents from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) before they could receive federal student aid.

The court vacated the policy in its entirety, meaning that Jay Treaty students should no longer be required to obtain green cards or other DHS documentation to access federal student aid.

The case challenged a policy change ED made when it quietly replaced a long-standing documentation framework that had allowed Jay Treaty students to demonstrate their eligibility using readily accessible documents such as band cards, birth records or Tribal affidavits. Without explanation, ED adopted new guidance requiring these students to instead produce DHS-issued immigration documents, such as a green card or temporary I-551 stamp, before they could access Title IV aid.

The court found that ED's new requirement was unlawful for two independent reasons: First, ED failed to adequately explain why it was abandoning its long-standing policy, making the change arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, and second, the new requirement exceeded ED's legal authority under the Higher Education Act, which does not require lawful permanent residents to submit immigration documents from the government to qualify for aid.

What the Decision Means

For those who work in federal Indian law, education law or Tribal advocacy, the decision provides meaningful support for the rights of Jay Treaty students and communities to which they belong. The court's statutory analysis confirms that American Indians born in Canada and deemed lawful permanent residents under the Immigration and Nationality Act cannot be subjected to additional immigration documentation requirements that the U.S. Congress did not authorize.

The court also rejected ED's attempts to shift blame for the students' injuries to their universities, holding that the policy itself was the cause of harm; students who were previously eligible for aid were effectively shut out when ED changed the rules without justification.

This is a precedent-setting victory for the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe and an important result for Jay Treaty students across the country.

description:

Today more than 250 organizations are demanding an independent investigation and clear rules so that protest never triggers immigration enforcement.
Clear public policies so that protest never leads to immigration enforcement, whatever a person’s status.

text:
On August 12, the Canada Border Services Agency checked the immigration status of international graduates at a student protest in Calgary and issued removal orders to 10. Today more than 250 organizations are demanding an independent investigation and clear rules so that protest never triggers immigration enforcement.

Over 250 major civil liberties, human rights, labour, faith, environmental, migrant, refugee and community organizations are uniting around a simple principle: migrants are part of our society movements and have the right to speak out without fear. Freedom of expression and peaceful assembly are protected by Section 2 of the Charter of rights and freedoms. Those rights belong to everyone in Canada, regardless of immigration status.

In an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, the organizations are making four demands: An independent investigation into the actions of Calgary Police and CBSA on August 12. Immediate suspension of the removal orders. Clear public policies so that protest never leads to immigration enforcement, whatever a person’s status. And process work permits for the Portage College graduates under the rules that applied when they enrolled.

Related: Canada illegally returning refugees to the U.S. amid widespread rights violations

“Migrants are part of every movement in this country,” said Bikramjit Singh of the PGWP Committee, member organization of the Migrant Rights Network. “What happened in Calgary was meant to frighten people into silence. It will not work. Migrants will keep organizing, and keep speaking out. We will defend those rights every time they are attacked.”

A migrant worker must be able to join a picket line. An international student must be able to protest government policy. Refugees and undocumented people must be able to demonstrate and organize. If basic rights are denied to some people then we further entrench their vulnerability and treat them as less than equal.

The protests arose after students graduated from vocational programs at Portage College campuses in Calgary and Edmonton. Those programs were eligible for a Post-Graduation Work Permit when they enrolled in 2024, and graduates of the same programs in earlier years received permits. On June 24, 2026, Immigration Canada added language to its website excluding “non-credit” programs and used it to refuse them. That term appears in no regulation, no Canada Gazette notice and no Ministerial Instruction before that date. As many as 1,500 graduates are affected. Hundreds have already been refused after paying more than $30,000 in tuition and completing their studies.

Newly uncovered emails show that students asked about their eligibility while still enrolled. Guidance provided by the federal government to the college said currently enrolled students would not be affected and told them to continue their programs. The correspondence was first reported by PressProgress.

“I followed every rule. I paid my tuition, completed my studies and graduated. When I enrolled, we understood that the program qualified for a post-graduation work permit. After we graduated, the federal government refused our applications. While students were peacefully protesting these refusals, several of our classmates were served with removal orders. We are asking the government to assess us fairly under the eligibility requirements communicated when we enrolled and to withdraw the removal orders while our cases are properly reviewed,” said Gurparas Singh, a Portage College graduate.

Police attended the protest reportedly over access to a sidewalk on August 12. According to CBSA’s own account, officers then checked 20 protesters, directed 12 to a CBSA office and issued 10 removal orders the same day. CBSA issued the orders while the students’ Federal Court challenges were still pending, and the students were within their 90-day restoration period. Officers also seized their passports.

Read the open letter with the full list of signatories, petition and guide: www.MigrantRights.ca/RightToProtest.

Statements from signatories

“We at Amnesty International Canada are appalled by the CBSA’s crackdown at a student protest in Calgary on August 12. People should not have to choose between speaking out against injustice and protecting their ability to remain in Canada. Targeting peaceful protests strikes fear into the heart of entire communities, making people think twice about speaking out in public, regardless of their immigration status or how long they’ve lived in Canada. It’s intimidation, pure and simple.”

– Julia Sande, Strategic Litigation, Refugee and Migrant Rights Campaigner, Amnesty International Canada

“A picket line cannot become an immigration checkpoint. Migrant workers must be able to confront a bad boss, join a strike and stand beside their co-workers without wondering whether speaking up could put their future in Canada at risk. What happened in Calgary is of deep concern to workers and every union in this country.”

–Mark Hancock, National President, Canadian Union of Public Employees

“At a time when Canada rightly stands up against the tyranny of President Trump, we cannot adopt the tactics of his ICE force. The freedom to protest is not real if some people can march without fear while others have to wonder whether an officer will ask for their immigration papers. It demands accountability and immediate protection for migrants exercising their rights. We urge for Canada to recommit itself to protecting the right to freedom of assembly and to distance itself from these kinds of ICE-esque tactics.”

–Steven Zhou, Spokesperson, National Council of Canadian Muslims

“Migrants and refugees in Canada already live the uncertainty of temporary or precarious status. They must be able to organize, protest and defend their rights without fear of putting their ability to remain here on the line. Immigration enforcement must not follow people into spaces where they are peacefully organizing for their rights. This goes to the heart of what our democracy means. The Canadian government should fix the injustice that brought these students into the streets and make sure immigration enforcement never becomes the response to migrant organizing.”

–Gauri Sreenivasan, Co-Executive Director, Canadian Council for Refugees

“The freedom to protest has to belong to everyone. Governments cannot praise democratic participation while allowing immigration enforcement to cast a shadow over who feels safe enough to march, organize and demand change. What happened in Calgary needs accountability and immediate protections for migrants exercising their rights.”

–Atiya Jaffar, Canada Country Manager, 350.org

“There is something profoundly unjust about people, raising their voices because they have been treated unfairly and then facing immigration enforcement for doing so. These persons were explicitly recruited and welcomed to migrate to contribute to the development and improvement of Canadian economy and society. No one should have to choose between speaking the truth about an injustice and remaining with their family and community in Canada. Unfortunately, this contributes further to the marginalization of the migrant sector in Canadian society, which silences too many important voices. The United Church of Canada finds this marginalization and oppression of voices unjust and supports actions to bring justice to these silenced voices.”

MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Protesters claim a hunger strike is ongoing at the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason, Tennessee, housing immigrants detained by ICE.
In a statement sent to WREG on Wednesday, an ICE spokesperson stated the following: “There is no hunger strike at the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason, Tennessee.

text:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Protesters claim a hunger strike is ongoing at the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason, Tennessee, housing immigrants detained by ICE. However, the prison is denying those claims.

A group of protesters marched Wednesday to the detention center, demanding change.

Advocacy group ‘Memphis 4 Revolutionary Socialism’ alleges detainees are being fed ‘inedible food’ and some have been ‘physically forced’ to sign deportation papers.

In a statement sent to WREG on Wednesday, an ICE spokesperson stated the following:

“There is no hunger strike at the West Tennessee Detention Facility in Mason, Tennessee.

Claims that there are subprime conditions at ICE detention centers or allegations of physical intimidation are FALSE. ICE is regularly audited and inspected by external agencies. All detainees are provided with 3 meals a day, clean water, clothing, bedding, showers, soap, and toiletries. Illegal aliens also have access to phones to communicate with their family members and lawyers. Certified dieticians evaluate meals. In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens.

It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody. This includes medical, dental, and mental health services as available, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives.“

Since August 30, Memphis 4 Revolutionary Socialism (M4RS), a political organization, said more than 400 immigrants in the detention center have been on hunger strike in response to deplorable conditions inside the facility and abusive tactics such as physical abuse to force detainees to sign papers.

The organization alleges that detainees are being forced to work in the kitchen daily, but currently, all the detainees are withholding their labor as they continue to go on hunger strike due to the nature of the conditions inside.

These claims come after more than 120 people were arrested during an ICE raid at a Berclair nightclub Sunday night, the Department of Homeland Security said on Tuesday.

The operation resulted in the arrests of offenders with criminal histories that include larceny, drug possession, domestic violence, driving while intoxicated, assault, child endangerment, and prostitution, DHS said.

This is not the first time that protesters have protested against the West Tennessee Detention Center, which has now been in operation for a year.

Terry Leggett, town administrator for Mason, said the ICE facility benefits the community.

“Well, I understand their dislike, but the majority of people that came out last month and protested, they don’t live in the city. They don’t benefit from the revenue that the city gets from having Core Civic here,” Leggett said. “And we have no control over who’s detained there or who operates it there. The police, I don’t know of a single call that we’ve made there in the last six months.”

“Well, the contract that was entered into last year with the Mayor was that the town will benefit by getting a dollar per day per detainee that is housed there. And that amounts to anywhere from $10,000 to $12,000 a month,” said Leggett. “I think their daily population right now is running about 450 to 470. CoreCivic on the population payment, that’s going to account for probably $120,000 to $140,000 a year in revenue. And the town only takes in less than $20,000 a month of sales tax.”

While there is support over the ICE detention center, there is also ongoing opposition, nearly a year since the facility began housing detainees.

“So if we really, truly want to make a difference, we also have to seek to organize in our workplaces to support in the best way possible and ensure that Core Civic is obsolete soon.,” said a protestor.

title: Vermont Prisons Agree to Improve Services for ICE Detainees After Discrimination Complaint
description:
Facing the prospect of a discrimination lawsuit, the Vermont Department of Corrections has agreed to provide federal immigration detainees in its prisons with better access to language interpretation, legal counsel and court hearings.
Immigration lawyers previously said the department restricted their ability to meet with federal detainees and that non-English speakers lacked language interpretation in state prisons.
Under the agreement, the department is required to ensure that immigration detainees are provided language interpretation services and regular access to immigration lawyers with the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project.
Federal immigration authorities use Vermont prisons to hold detainees, often more than a dozen at a time.
Murad previously defended his decision to end routine meetings between VAAP attorneys and immigration detainees.
text:
Facing the prospect of a discrimination lawsuit, the Vermont Department of Corrections has agreed to provide federal immigration detainees in its prisons with better access to language interpretation, legal counsel and court hearings.

The Vermont Human Rights Commission announced Tuesday it had reached a settlement with the department, following a discrimination complaint the commission filed in January.

Immigration lawyers previously said the department restricted their ability to meet with federal detainees and that non-English speakers lacked language interpretation in state prisons.

With the settlement, the Corrections Department is resolving the discrimination complaint before it’s brought to civil court, according to Lauri Fisher, general counsel for the department.

Under the agreement, the department is required to ensure that immigration detainees are provided language interpretation services and regular access to immigration lawyers with the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project. The settlement does not include a monetary sum.

“It’s the one time I’d say, ‘I was pleased we got sued,’ because it made us better,” Fisher said in an interview Tuesday.

Federal immigration authorities use Vermont prisons to hold detainees, often more than a dozen at a time. Though detainees can be held in any state prison, they’re most commonly taken to Chittenden Regional Correctional Facility in South Burlington or Northwest State Correctional Facility in St. Albans Town.

The settlement marks a resolution between the Corrections Department and advocates for immigrants’ legal rights, who have been at odds after lawyers with the asylum assistance project alleged earlier this year that the department was impeding their access to detainees.

Their clients also weren’t receiving interpretation services, lawyers alleged in March, leaving immigrants to go without proper medical care or be disciplined without understanding why.

Language interpretation for people who are detained is essential to provide access to services they have a legal right to receive, said Erin Jacobsen, VAAP’s advocacy director.

“And if you can’t do that, then rights might as well just be wishes,” Jacobsen said.

Issues with language and attorney access began, immigration lawyers alleged, after Commissioner Jon Murad took over the department in August 2025.

Murad previously defended his decision to end routine meetings between VAAP attorneys and immigration detainees. He said in March he was enforcing the department’s policies and cutting off practices that shouldn’t have been allowed under his predecessor.

Fisher said Tuesday that the department hasn’t changed its position since March, rather that it’s changing its rules and policies.

Previous policies were limiting, she said. Now the department has taken the opportunity to “grow” by following the recommendations of VAAP and the American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont, according to Fisher.

“We’re just modifying (department policies) to adapt to modern times, if you will,” Fisher said.

Under the agreement, the department will be required to identify someone’s preferred language when they’re taken into a facility. Then, prison and medical staff will be required to use a mobile interpreter to communicate with people in their preferred language.

If someone’s preferred language isn’t English, the person can’t be disciplined for disobeying an instruction given in English, according to the settlement.

Along with guarantees for language access, the department is directed to provide the asylum assistance project with a daily list of all immigration detainees in state prisons, according to the settlement.

Under the agreement, a group of attorneys with the legal organization are allowed to go into the prisons in South Burlington and St. Albans Town every other week to meet with a group of detainees. Those attorneys will be able to use prison tablets for interpretation, and they’ll be allowed to bring in laptops or other devices after they’re inspected by corrections staff.

The arrangement mimics how VAAP lawyers previously operated before last fall.

Many of the changes mandated by the settlement began during the months of negotiation, according to Jacobsen, but the legal agreement requires that the department’s policies be updated.

If the department doesn’t abide by the agreement there could be further legal action, but Jacobsen said the department has been cooperative.

“I am not imagining that this is going to be a problem,” she said.

___

text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked Virginia from enforcing key provisions of a new law restricting cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities, allowing existing partnerships with U.S. Immigration and Customs enforcement to continue while the legal challenge plays out.

Senior U.S. District Court Judge Robert Payne in Richmond issued a preliminary injunction Monday, barring the commonwealth from applying the law against federal immigration officers, employees or agencies and from interfering with existing agreements under Section 287(g) of federal immigration law.

Those agreements allow ICE to authorize trained state and local officers to perform certain federal immigration enforcement duties.

Virginia’s law required existing agreements to be rewritten by Sept. 1 to include a dozen conditions governing how federal immigration operations could be conducted around the state. Agreements that were not modified would have been considered void and unenforceable.

However, Payne left one significant restriction in place, preventing localities and law enforcement agencies that have never participated in the 287(g) program from entering such agreements for the first time.

Attorney General Jay Jones said Tuesday that his office would immediately seek to keep the injunction from taking effect while appealing the court’s decision.

“My office strongly disagrees with the judge’s order and will urgently file a motion to stay this ruling and appeal the temporary injunction,” Jones said in an email.

Jones argued that the ruling misinterprets both contract law and the state’s authority over its local governments. Because the conditions apply to Virginia’s localities rather than ICE, they do not directly regulate federal immigration enforcement, he said.

Jones also cited Dillon’s Rule, arguing that Virginia’s legislature has the authority to modify or withdraw localities’ power to enter contracts.

“The General Assembly was well within its legal authority to pass this law and to put statutory requirements in place to ensure Virginia’s already resource-constrained localities and law enforcement agencies are not devoting critical resources toward carrying out responsibilities that rest solely with the federal government,” Jones said.

Judge finds federal government likely to prevail

The U.S. Justice Department sued Virginia in June, arguing that the law unconstitutionally interferes with federal immigration enforcement and impairs existing contracts between ICE and Virginia localities.

In granting the injunction, Payne found the federal government was likely to prevail on its claim that the law violates the U.S. Constitution’s Contract Clause.

He concluded that the new requirements created a “substantial impairment” of existing agreements and were not appropriately and reasonably tailored to advance a significant and legitimate public purpose.

The federal government was also likely to succeed on its Supremacy Clause claim, Payne found, writing that the Virginia law “directly regulates the conduct of federal law enforcement” in an area under federal authority.

Without an injunction, the judge concluded, the federal government would likely suffer irreparable harm from both the impairment of its contracts and interference with its immigration responsibilities. He also found that temporarily blocking the law was in the public interest.

However, the four-page order does not resolve the lawsuit or permanently strike down the statute. Payne wrote the court would lay out its reasoning in “a forthcoming memorandum opinion.”

The injunction will remain in place while the case proceeds or until the court orders otherwise.

Background of the new law

Virginia lawmakers adopted the restrictions this year through Senate Bill 783, sponsored by Sen. Saddam Azlan Salim, D-Fairfax, and identical House Bill 1441 by Del. Alfonso Lopez, D-Arlington. Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed both measures in April, and they became law July 1.

In addition to placing conditions on 287(g) agreements, the legislation generally prohibits state and local officers from assisting with federal civil immigration operations. Exceptions include assistance permitted or required by law, authorized by a judicial warrant or subpoena, or involving the transfer of an adult from a correctional facility after receipt of an immigration detainer.

For existing 287(g) agreements, the new law requires a dozen conditions, including advance identification of participating federal agents and restrictions on enforcement at schools, faith-based organizations, courthouses and polling places. It also imposes limits on surveillance technology and requires judicial warrants for entering homes and making certain information requests.

Legal advocates respond

The Legal Aid Justice Center, which filed a friend-of-the-court brief supporting Virginia, said the General Assembly acted within its constitutional authority by placing conditions on what the organization described as a voluntary federal program.

“We are very concerned that existing 287(g) agreements will be allowed to continue,” the organization said in a statement Tuesday. “These agreements entangle local law enforcement in federal immigration enforcement, which undermines the trust communities need to report crimes and cooperate with investigations.”

While welcoming the portion of the ruling that prevents new agreements, the center argued that Payne went further than the federal government requested by barring Virginia from interfering with existing agreements “in any way.”

The organization said that language could put related actions by local governments beyond the oversight of state lawmakers and Virginia voters, and it urged the state to appeal and seek a stay.

Monica Sarmiento, executive director of the Virginia Coalition for Immigrant Rights, said her group was “deeply disappointed” by Payne’s ruling.

She pointed to videos recorded by residents showing what she described as combative and aggressive ICE encounters in recent months.

“Virginia voters overwhelmingly support the initiative to restrict local law enforcement from collaborating with ICE,” Sarmiento said.

Immigration enforcement in Virginia accelerates

The legal dispute is unfolding as federal immigration authorities step up enforcement in Virginia and neighboring Maryland.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said a sweeping ICE operation resulted in 1,328 arrests across the two states between Aug. 1 and Aug. 14.

According to the agency, those arrested included people with convictions or prior arrests involving sexual battery, kidnapping, driving while intoxicated, identity theft, robbery, murder, attempted murder and rape.

DHS did not say how many of the detainees had been convicted of crimes.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the operation targeted people he characterized as threats to public safety.

“Over the course of just two weeks in Virginia and Maryland, they arrested sexual assailants, kidnappers, drunk drivers, robbers, and gang members,” Mullin said in a statement.

Much of the operation focused on the Washington suburbs, according to ICE, although officers carried out targeted enforcement actions elsewhere in Virginia and Maryland.

Spanberger, meanwhile, has taken several steps since entering office in January to distance state agencies from federal civil immigration enforcement. In February, she directed state law enforcement agencies to terminate their 287(g) agreements, though the directive did not apply to agreements involving local agencies.

Her Executive Order 16, issued in May, directed state agencies and institutions to develop guidance for employees who encounter federal immigration officers at schools, hospitals, courthouses, polling places and commonwealth attorneys’ offices.

The order also prohibits nonpublic state property from being used as a staging area, processing location or operational base for federal civil immigration enforcement and requires agencies to verify that federal officers seeking access possess a valid warrant or order.

Spanberger cited data showing “approximately 70 percent of individuals booked in detention centers in Virginia have not been convicted of a crime” in the May directive.

Payne directed the state to distribute Monday’s ruling to commonwealth’s attorneys across the state and ordered the parties to to contact the court to schedule further proceedings.

Jones said his office would continue defending the new law as the case moves forward.

“Accordingly, my team will continue to vigorously defend this law to ensure that state and local law enforcement are focused on their core responsibilities of investigating and deterring criminal activity, staffing correctional facilities, and engaging with their communities, not forced to be foot soldiers of an overreaching federal government,” Jones said.

text:
WASHINGTON – Ranking Member Ilhan Omar (MN-05) delivered the following opening statement at today’s Workforce Protections Subcommittee hearing entitled, “Less Red Tape, More Opportunity: Unleashing American Workers and Job Creators.”

“Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you to our witnesses for joining us today.

“My Republican colleagues love to talk about getting rid of red tape, but let’s look at what they actually want to get rid of: it is the light at a construction site; it is the respirator a worker wears to protect themselves from asbestos exposure; it is an inspector looking at a mine and simply asking a coal operator whether the roof is going to hold.

“Every one of these commonsense rules is on the books because a worker was hurt or killed on the job. And this country decided it would not let it happen again.

“But now the Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans are trying to repeal them.

“They have also fired staff across the Department of Labor and weakened important safety agencies like the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

“The attacks on workplace protections have made it harder to hold bad employ[ers] accountable, and harder for workers to trust that someone has their back.

“Now, 2025 was a very good year for President Trump personally.

“According to his own federal disclosure forms, Trump received 2.2 billion dollars in income after returning to the White House.

“Let me put that in perspective: the median American worker would have to work over forty-three thousand years to earn what President Trump made in a single year in office. Forty-three thousand years.

“While working families were falling further behind on their bills, the man in the Oval Office is cashing in. And Congressional Republicans are just looking the other way.

“Worse, they actually added red tape of their own to the very programs all of these families need to survive.

“In the year since this Republican Congress passed the ‘Big Ugly Bill,’ more than eight million Americans have lost their health coverage and more than four million lost food assistance.

“Republicans know they don’t have a good economic record to run on. But let’s be clear about the plan they are offering to the American people: it is more red tape [and] hardship for you, and less of it for their corporate beneficiaries.

“Instead of crafting an agenda that helps working people with the cost of living, Committee Republicans have consistently chosen to take the wrong priorities.

“They have chosen to make labor cheap.

“That is what their bills would do: making it easier for an employer to treat a worker like an independent contractor instead of a full-time employee; letting employers off the hook for wage theft; and making overtime cheaper and worth less for the workers putting in the time.

“And they have chosen to make jobs more dangerous.

“Just last month, Committee Republicans voted to block OSHA from ever issuing any standard [protecting] workers from extreme heat – in one of the hottest summers in our country’s history.

“Just as troubling is what they have chosen not to do. This Committee has held zero hearings on issues that working people in my district and across the country care about most: not one hearing on raising the minimum wage; not one hearing on addressing the violence in the workplace; and not one hearing on our child labor laws, even as this Administration announced a plan to weaken them for 14-year-olds.

“Mr. Chair, every worker in America deserves to come home safe at the end of the day. That should be one of the most basic obligations we have to our constituents.

“Working families are not asking for much. They are asking for a fair shot, an honest wage, and a safe workplace.

“But this Congress, and this Administration, are failing to meet the moment.

“Stripping away labor protections will not unleash anything good.

“It will just move the cost of doing business onto the bodies and livelihoods of working-class people who do the real work that powers this economy.

“Working Americans deserve a government that works for them, not corporate interests.

“Thank you, and I yield back.”
